01_Measurement_and_solution_language.jso.title: Measurement and solution language
01_Measurement_and_solution_language.jso.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Select the correct apparatus (stopwatch, thermometer, balance, burette, pipette, measuring cylinder or gas syringe) for a stated measurement, matching the instrument to the physical quantity being measured and the precision needed.
Define solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue and filtrate, and use these terms correctly to describe a filtration in context.

prerequisites.statement: Describe the three states of matter (solid, liquid, gas) and recognise that a change of state does not change the identity of the substance.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Matching an instrument to a measurement starts with knowing whether the sample is a solid, a liquid or a gas, since that already rules several instruments out.

prerequisites.statement: Read the value shown by a pointer or a liquid level against a linear graduated scale (for example on a ruler or a thermometer).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every instrument named in this lesson is only as good as the reading taken from its scale; without this skill, choosing the 'right' apparatus still gives an unreliable result.

diagnostic_items.question: A measuring cylinder with 1 cm³ divisions is filled with liquid up to the mark between 36 and 37 cm³, nearer to 37. What volume should be recorded, and how should your eye be positioned to read it?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: 37 cm³, read with the eye level with the bottom of the curved liquid surface (the meniscus), not from above or below it.

common_wrong_answers.answer: 36.5 cm³, read from directly above the cylinder
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner averages the two nearest marks instead of reading the nearer one, and reads from above the liquid, which introduces a parallax error instead of removing it.

common_wrong_answers.answer: 37 cm³, read from eye level with the top of the meniscus curve
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reads the correct value here by chance but uses the top of the curved surface rather than the flat bottom of the meniscus, which is not reliable once the curve is more pronounced.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can both read the nearest graduation accurately and knows the eye-level/meniscus convention that makes any volume scale reading repeatable between people.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Place the cylinder on a flat surface, crouch or lower the cylinder until your eye is exactly level with the liquid surface, and read the scale value at the bottom of the curved meniscus.

theory_blocks.title: Choose the instrument from the quantity, not from its appearance
theory_blocks.body:
Before picking any apparatus, ask one question: what physical quantity actually needs a number? Mass needs a balance. Time needs a stopwatch. Temperature needs a thermometer.

The volume of a liquid needs a pipette, burette or measuring cylinder, depending on how exact that volume must be.

The volume of a gas produced by a reaction needs a gas syringe (or, as an alternative, a measuring cylinder filled with water and turned upside down in a trough, so the gas collects at the top by pushing the water out) — never a liquid-volume instrument used the normal way up,

even though gas syringes and some cylinders can look superficially similar on a bench.

Two instruments that look alike (a measuring cylinder and a burette, say) can still be completely wrong substitutes for each other, because 'looks like a graduated tube' is not the same property as 'is precise enough for this job'.

[[blue:Always name the quantity first]], then choose the tool that measures exactly that quantity to the precision the task needs.

theory_blocks.title: The core instruments and what each one actually measures
theory_blocks.body:
| Instrument | Measures | Typical reading |
|---|---|---|
| Balance | mass | to the nearest 0.1 g or 0.01 g |
| Thermometer | temperature | to the nearest 1 °C or 0.5 °C |
| Stopwatch | time | to the nearest 0.1 s or 1 s |
| Measuring cylinder | an approximate liquid volume | to the nearest 1 cm³ (coarse divisions) |
| Volumetric pipette | one fixed, accurate liquid volume | a single marked volume, e.g. 25.0 cm³ |
| Burette | a variable, precisely controlled liquid volume | to the nearest 0.1 cm³, released through a tap |
| Gas syringe | the volume of a gas | to the nearest 1 cm³, as the plunger is pushed out |

The pipette and the burette both measure liquid volume far more precisely than a measuring cylinder, but they do different jobs: a pipette always delivers the *same* volume every time it is used, while a burette can deliver *any* chosen volume, a little at a time, because the tap lets the flow be stopped exactly when needed.

A measuring cylinder is read once and is good enough only when an approximate volume is acceptable.

theory_blocks.title: Solvent, solute, solution and saturation
theory_blocks.body:
When a solid dissolves in a liquid, the liquid doing the dissolving is the **solvent** and the substance that dissolves is the **solute**. The mixture that results, in which the solute is no longer visible as separate particles, is the **solution**.

At a given temperature, a solvent can only dissolve a limited mass of a particular solute. A solution that has dissolved the maximum amount possible at a stated temperature is a **saturated solution**: adding more solute at that same temperature leaves the extra solute undissolved.

Because solubility changes with temperature (most solids dissolve more as temperature rises), a solution saturated at one temperature is not necessarily saturated, or even still fully dissolved, at another.

The phrase 'saturated solution' is therefore only a complete statement once a temperature is attached to it.

theory_blocks.title: Filtration: naming residue and filtrate correctly
theory_blocks.body:
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (or from a solution) by passing the mixture through filter paper held in a funnel.

1. Fold the filter paper into a cone and place it inside the funnel, resting the funnel in the neck of a collecting beaker or flask.
2. Pour the mixture gently into the paper cone; do not overfill above the paper's rim.
3. The insoluble solid is trapped by the tiny pores in the paper and stays behind: this trapped solid is the **residue**.
4. The liquid (or solution) passes through the pores and drips into the collecting vessel below: this collected liquid is the **filtrate**.

The two terms are defined purely by where each part ends up, never by what the substance 'usually' is.

If sand is filtered from salty water, the sand is the residue and the salty water is the filtrate — but if that filtrate is later evaporated, the dry salt crystals that appear are a *new* residue of that second step,

even though the same word 'salt' is involved throughout.

assets.caption: Filtration of an insoluble solid from a liquid: the mixture is poured down into the paper cone, the solid is trapped on the filter paper as the residue, and the liquid passes through into the beaker as the filtrate.
assets.purpose: Make the residue/filtrate distinction visible by location, not by what substance it happens to be, so the terms transfer correctly to any new mixture.

theory_blocks.title: The same word, a different stage
theory_blocks.body:
Residue and filtrate name a [[blue:*role in one particular step*]], not a fixed identity for a substance. Consider filtering a mixture of insoluble chalk powder and salt water: the chalk is the residue, and the salty filtrate passes through.

If that filtrate is now heated so the water evaporates, dry salt crystals appear in the evaporating dish — and that dry salt is correctly called a residue too, even though earlier in the same investigation 'salt' was dissolved inside the filtrate.

Always ask 'residue or filtrate of *which* step?' rather than assuming the word always points at the same physical substance.

theory_blocks.title: Where this is used next
theory_blocks.body:
Titration (the next lesson) reuses the pipette and burette from this lesson's apparatus table, now both in the same investigation: a pipette delivers a fixed volume of one solution into a flask, and a burette delivers a controlled, measured volume of a second solution into it.

Later lessons on separation reuse filtration itself, now as one step inside a longer method (for example, filtering an insoluble solid before crystallising a dissolved one from the filtrate).

Getting the vocabulary and the apparatus choice exactly right here avoids every later lesson having to re-teach it.

keywords.definition: The substance, usually a liquid, that dissolves another substance to form a solution.
The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution.
A mixture formed when a solute dissolves completely in a solvent, with no visible separate particles.
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at a stated temperature.
A solid substance that remains after evaporation, distillation, filtration or any similar process (in filtration, the solid left on the filter paper).
The liquid that passes through filter paper and is collected during filtration.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube, read at eye level to take an accurate volume reading.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing instruments for three measurements.** A student investigating a reaction between a metal and an acid needs to record: (i) the mass of the dry metal sample before the reaction, (ii) the time taken until bubbling stops, and (iii) the volume of gas collected during the reaction. State the most suitable apparatus for each.
knowns: Quantity (i): mass of a solid
Quantity (ii): a time interval
Quantity (iii): the volume of a gas
unknowns: The correct instrument for each of the three quantities
reasoning: (i) Mass of a solid sample is measured directly with a balance; no other listed instrument measures mass.
(ii) A time interval, from the reaction starting to the bubbling stopping, is measured with a stopwatch.

(iii) The volume of gas produced is collected and read from a gas syringe: the gas pushes the plunger out and the volume is read from the scale.

(An upturned measuring cylinder full of water in a trough would also work, but the gas syringe is the standard answer.)
worked_examples.solution: (i) Balance. (ii) Stopwatch. (iii) Gas syringe.
worked_examples.interpretation: Each choice follows directly from naming the quantity first: once 'mass', 'time' and 'gas volume' are identified separately, only one instrument in the list matches each one.

worked_examples.statement: **Naming residue and filtrate in a two-step separation.** A mixture of insoluble sand and salt water is filtered. The filtrate from this filtration is then heated gently until all the water evaporates. State what collects on the filter paper, what is collected underneath it, and what is left in the evaporating dish at the very end — using the correct term for each.
knowns: Sand is insoluble in water; salt is soluble in water
Filtration step: mixture poured through filter paper
Evaporation step: the liquid collected from filtration is then heated to dryness
unknowns: The correct name for the solid on the filter paper
The correct name for the liquid collected below it
The correct name for the solid left after evaporation
reasoning: Sand does not dissolve, so it is trapped by the filter paper: this makes sand the residue of the filtration step.
The salt stays dissolved in the water that passes through the paper, so that salt solution is the filtrate of the filtration step.

When the filtrate (the salt solution) is evaporated, the water leaves as vapour and the salt that remains behind in the dish is a residue again — this time, the residue of the evaporation step, not of the filtration step.
worked_examples.solution: Filter paper: sand (the residue of filtration). Collected underneath: salt solution (the filtrate of filtration). Left in the dish after evaporation: dry salt crystals (the residue of evaporation).
worked_examples.interpretation: The same word, 'residue', correctly describes two different solids here, because it names a role within a specific step, not a fixed label for one substance.

worked_examples.statement: **Deciding whether a solution is saturated.** Beaker 1 contains a sugar solution at room temperature with some undissolved sugar visible at the bottom. Beaker 2 contains a clear sugar solution, with no visible solid, that was made hot and has just been allowed to cool to the same room temperature. Can beaker 1 be called 'saturated'? Can beaker 2? Explain, and state what extra information would resolve beaker 2.
knowns: Beaker 1: undissolved solid visible at a stated temperature (room temperature)
Beaker 2: no visible solid, but was previously hotter and has since cooled
unknowns: Whether each solution is saturated at room temperature
reasoning: Beaker 1 has visible undissolved solute at a clearly stated temperature (room temperature), which is exactly the definition of a solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature: it is saturated at room temperature.

Beaker 2 has no visible solid, but that alone does not prove anything: because most solids dissolve less as temperature falls,

the solution could now be holding more dissolved solute than it could normally dissolve at room temperature (supersaturated and not yet crystallised), exactly saturated, or still unsaturated.

Without comparing the actual mass of sugar dissolved in beaker 2 to the known solubility of sugar at room temperature, or waiting to see whether crystals eventually appear, beaker 2 cannot be classified from appearance alone.
worked_examples.solution:
Beaker 1: saturated at room temperature (confirmed by the visible undissolved excess). Beaker 2: cannot be classified from appearance alone;

the mass of dissolved sugar would need to be compared with the known solubility of sugar at room temperature, or the solution watched to see whether excess solute crystallises out.
worked_examples.interpretation: Visible undissolved solute is sufficient evidence for 'saturated'; its absence is not sufficient evidence for 'unsaturated', because a cooled solution can hold onto more dissolved solute than normal before it eventually crystallises.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that no visible solid automatically means a solution is not saturated, when a recently cooled solution can in fact be holding more than its normal saturation amount.

worked_examples.statement: **An apparatus-and-vocabulary station.** A technician sets up three stations. Station A requires a liquid to be measured out at exactly 25.0 cm³ every time, for several repeat experiments. Station B requires between 0 and 20 cm³ of a solution to be added drop by drop until a colour change is seen. Station C requires an insoluble powder to be separated from the solution it is stirred into. For each station, name the correct apparatus or technique, and state which term — residue, filtrate, solute, solvent or solution — applies to each labelled part of station C's outcome.
knowns: Station A: the same fixed volume is needed repeatedly
Station B: a variable, controlled volume added dropwise until an observable change
Station C: separating an insoluble powder from the liquid it was stirred into
unknowns: Apparatus for stations A and B
Technique and correct vocabulary for station C
reasoning: Station A needs the same exact volume every time: this is exactly what a volumetric pipette is designed for, since it is calibrated to deliver one fixed volume accurately.
Station B needs a variable volume added a little at a time, stopped at an observed change: this is exactly what a burette (with its tap) is designed for.

Station C separates an insoluble solid from the liquid it is stirred into by filtration; before filtering, the liquid is the solvent,

the powder is the solute only if it had actually dissolved — but since the powder is insoluble, it never became a solute or part of a solution at all, it simply remained a separate solid suspended in the liquid.
After filtering station C's mixture: the powder trapped on the paper is the residue, and the liquid collected underneath is the filtrate.
worked_examples.solution: Station A: volumetric pipette (25.0 cm³). Station B: burette. Station C: filtration; the powder is the residue and the collected liquid is the filtrate. Because the powder is insoluble, the terms solute/solvent/solution do not apply to it at all.
worked_examples.interpretation: The exam question tests whether 'solute' is only applied correctly to a substance that has actually dissolved; an insoluble solid in a liquid is never a solute, so it is wrong to force the solution vocabulary onto every mixture.

guided_exercises.statement: A student needs to measure: (a) the temperature change when a solid dissolves in water, (b) exactly 25.0 cm³ of a solution to transfer into a flask, and (c) the time taken for a colour change to occur. Name the correct apparatus for each.
hints: Identify the physical quantity in each part before choosing an instrument — do not let 'measuring something in cm³' distract you from what is actually fixed or variable here.
Part (b) asks for the *same exact* volume every time, which should point you towards one specific instrument rather than a general-purpose one.
Part (c) is a time interval, measured from one clearly stated moment to another.
common_errors: Choosing a measuring cylinder for part (b) because it also measures volume, missing that a *fixed, repeated, accurate* volume is specifically what a pipette is for.

guided_exercises.statement: Insoluble chalk powder is stirred into salt water, then filtered. The filtrate from this filtration is then evaporated to dryness. Label each of the following with the correct term (residue, filtrate, solute, solvent or solution, as appropriate), explaining each choice: (i) the chalk powder before filtering, (ii) the chalk powder after filtering, (iii) the liquid collected after filtering, (iv) the dry salt left after evaporation.
hints: Decide first whether chalk ever dissolves in water at all — this decides whether 'solute' can ever apply to it.
'Residue' and 'filtrate' only make sense once you specify which step (filtration, or the later evaporation) you mean.
The salt dissolved in the water is behaving very differently from the chalk powder throughout — treat them separately.
guided_exercises.answer: (i) Before filtering, the chalk is simply an insoluble solid suspended in the salt solution; it is not a solute, because it never dissolves. (ii) After filtering, the chalk on the paper is the residue of the filtration step. (iii) The liquid collected underneath is the filtrate of the filtration step (a salt solution: water is the solvent, dissolved salt is the solute). (iv) After evaporating that filtrate, the dry salt left behind is the residue of the evaporation step.
common_errors: Calling the chalk powder a 'solute' because it is mixed into a liquid, even though it never actually dissolves.
Using 'residue' only once for the whole investigation, instead of recognising that filtration and evaporation each produce their own residue.

exercises.statement: A student is asked to add roughly 20 cm³ of water to dilute a solution, where the exact volume does not matter as long as it is close to 20 cm³. State which instrument is most suitable, and explain why a burette or pipette would not be a sensible choice here.
hints: Consider what level of precision the task actually needs, not what the most precise instrument available is.
Burettes and pipettes take longer to use and are usually reserved for tasks that specifically need high accuracy.
exercises.answer: A measuring cylinder is most suitable. A burette or pipette would give unnecessary precision for a task that only needs an approximate volume, and would simply slow the procedure down without improving the result.
exercises.full_solution: The task states the exact volume does not matter, only that it should be close to 20 cm³: this is precisely the situation a measuring cylinder (coarse divisions, quick to use) is designed for. A pipette only delivers one single fixed volume it is calibrated for, and a burette is designed for controlled, gradual delivery to a specific end point — both are the wrong tool when only an approximate volume is required.
common_errors: Assuming the 'most precise' instrument is always the 'best' choice, regardless of what the task actually needs.

exercises.statement: Copper sulfate solid is added to water at 25 °C, with stirring, until no more will dissolve and a small amount of undissolved blue solid remains visible at the bottom of the beaker. (a) Name the solvent, the solute and the resulting solution. (b) State whether this solution is saturated, and justify your answer using the correct definition.
hints: Identify which substance is doing the dissolving and which substance is being dissolved before naming anything else.
Check your answer to (b) against the full definition of 'saturated', which must include a temperature.
exercises.answer: (a) Solvent: water. Solute: copper sulfate. Solution: copper sulfate solution. (b) Yes, saturated at 25 °C: visible undissolved copper sulfate at a stated temperature (25 °C) confirms no more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
exercises.full_solution: Water is the substance doing the dissolving (solvent); copper sulfate is the substance being dissolved (solute); together they form a copper sulfate solution. Because solid copper sulfate remains visibly undissolved after thorough stirring, and the temperature (25 °C) is explicitly stated, the solution meets the full definition of saturated at that temperature.
common_errors: Stating the solution is saturated without repeating the temperature, leaving the claim incomplete.

exercises.statement: A measuring cylinder's smallest division is 1 cm³ (so a reading can be trusted to about ±0.5 cm³), while a particular volumetric pipette is accurate to ±0.06 cm³. By roughly what factor is the pipette more precise than the cylinder for this comparison?
hints: Divide the cylinder's uncertainty by the pipette's uncertainty.
The uncertainties are only given to 1 significant figure, so a rough answer (about 8) is all the data justify; 8.3 is also acceptable.
exercises.answer: About 8.3 times more precise (0.5 ÷ 0.06 ≈ 8.3).
exercises.full_solution: Factor = cylinder uncertainty ÷ pipette uncertainty = 0.5 cm³ ÷ 0.06 cm³ ≈ 8.3. This single number is the kind of evidence that justifies choosing a pipette over a cylinder whenever a measurement must be reliable to a fraction of a cm³, such as before a titration.
common_errors: Dividing the two uncertainties the wrong way round (0.06 ÷ 0.5), which gives a fraction less than 1 and wrongly suggests the cylinder is more precise.

exercises.statement: A new mixture is prepared: insoluble chalk dust is stirred into a sugar solution. The mixture is filtered, and the clear filtrate collected is then evaporated to dryness in an evaporating dish. (a) Identify every residue and every filtrate produced across the whole procedure, naming the step each one belongs to. (b) State which substances, if any, were ever solutes, and why.
hints: List the steps in order first (filtration, then evaporation), and decide what is produced at the end of each one, separately.
Decide whether chalk dust ever dissolves in the sugar solution before deciding whether it can be called a solute.
exercises.answer: (a) Filtration step: residue = chalk dust; filtrate = sugar solution. Evaporation step: residue = dry sugar crystals (there is no filtrate in an evaporation step, since nothing is being filtered). (b) Only sugar was ever a solute, because only sugar actually dissolved in the water; chalk dust remained an insoluble solid suspended in the liquid and was never dissolved, so it is never correctly called a solute.
exercises.full_solution: Tracing each step separately: filtration produces one residue (chalk, trapped on the paper) and one filtrate (sugar solution, passing through). That filtrate is then evaporated; evaporation is a different technique from filtration, so it produces its own residue (dry sugar) but no filtrate of its own, since nothing is passed through a filter in that step. Sugar is the only solute throughout, since it is the only substance that was ever genuinely dissolved; chalk is never a solute, even though it is mixed into a liquid, because it never dissolves.
common_errors: Calling the dry sugar crystals the 'filtrate' of the evaporation step, when evaporation produces a residue, not a filtrate, since no filtering happens in that step.

exam_questions.statement: A student carries out an investigation into a reaction between magnesium and dilute acid. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the mass of magnesium ribbon before the reaction. (b) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of hydrogen gas produced. (c) Name the apparatus used to measure the time from mixing the reagents to the reaction stopping. (d) Explain, in terms of what is actually measured, why an empty measuring cylinder standing the normal way up on the bench could not be used in place of your answer to part (b).
hints: Parts (a)-(c) each ask for one specific instrument matched to one specific quantity.
Part (d) wants a reason based on what substance is in the cylinder versus what substance is being produced, not just 'because it's the wrong shape'.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Balance. (b) Gas syringe. (c) Stopwatch. (d) A measuring cylinder used the normal way up measures the volume of a liquid poured into it; it is open at the top and cannot trap a gas as it is produced, so the hydrogen would simply escape and its volume could not be read. (It could only be used for a gas if filled with water and inverted in a trough, so the gas displaces the water.)
exam_questions.full_solution: (a)-(c) follow directly from matching mass, gas volume and time each to their correct instrument. (d): hydrogen gas is produced continuously as the reaction proceeds and must be collected in a closed space and its volume read as it pushes out the plunger of a gas syringe (or displaces water from an upturned, water-filled measuring cylinder); an open measuring cylinder standing the normal way up has no way to trap the escaping gas, so it simply cannot perform this measurement at all, regardless of its precision.
mark_scheme: Balance named for part (a) (1 mark).
Gas syringe named for part (b) (1 mark).
Stopwatch named for part (c) (1 mark).
States that a measuring cylinder cannot capture/collect an escaping gas, so it cannot measure a gas volume at all (1 mark).
Links the explanation specifically to hydrogen gas being produced and needing to be captured, not just a general statement that cylinders are 'for liquids' (1 mark).
common_errors: Explaining part (d) only as 'a cylinder is for liquids, not gases' without stating that the problem is capturing an escaping gas at all.

exam_questions.statement: A mixture of insoluble sulfur powder and a sodium chloride solution is filtered, and the filtrate is then evaporated until dry crystals remain. (a) State the correct term for the sulfur after filtering. (b) State the correct term for the liquid collected during filtering, and name its solute and its solvent. (c) State the correct term for the dry solid remaining after evaporation, and explain why this is not the same material, in role, as your answer to part (a), even though both are described using the same term.
hints: Keep the filtration step and the evaporation step completely separate when assigning terms.
Part (c) wants an explanation of the *role* each solid plays, not just a repeat of what each solid is made of.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Residue (of filtration). (b) Filtrate (of filtration); solute = sodium chloride; solvent = water. (c) Residue (of evaporation); although both (a) and (c) are called 'residue', (a) is an insoluble solid that was never dissolved and was simply trapped by filtration, while (c) is a solid that was fully dissolved earlier and only reappears as a solid once the solvent has been evaporated away.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Sulfur never dissolves in the solution, so after filtering it is simply the solid trapped on the filter paper: the residue of filtration. (b) The liquid passing through the paper is the filtrate; within it, sodium chloride (dissolved) is the solute and water (doing the dissolving) is the solvent. (c) Evaporating the filtrate removes the water, leaving the sodium chloride behind as a solid again — this is the residue of the evaporation step. The key difference from part (a) is that the sulfur residue was never dissolved at all, while the evaporation residue had been fully dissolved and only becomes solid once its solvent is removed.
mark_scheme: Residue correctly named in part (a) (1 mark).
Filtrate, solute (sodium chloride) and solvent (water) all correctly named in part (b) (2 marks).
Residue correctly named again in part (c) (1 mark).
Explanation in part (c) correctly distinguishes 'never dissolved' from 'was dissolved and then separated out again' (2 marks).
common_errors: Treating parts (a) and (c) as identical simply because both use the word 'residue', without explaining the different history of each solid.

challenge_questions.statement: **Planning the apparatus to follow a reaction's rate.** A student wants to find out how fast a gas is produced in a reaction, by recording the total volume of gas collected at regular time intervals rather than only at the end. (a) Name the instrument used for each of the two quantities being measured, and describe how the reaction flask must be connected so that none of the gas is lost. (b) The laboratory has no gas syringe. Describe the alternative arrangement built from a measuring cylinder, and state what must be inside that cylinder before the reaction starts. (c) The reaction chosen is marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid, which produces carbon dioxide. Explain why the arrangement in part (b) would give volumes that are too small for this particular reaction, and name a gas for which the same arrangement would work well.
hints: Name the physical quantity before the instrument: one measurement here is a volume of gas, the other is a time interval, and both have to be taken at the same moments.
For part (b), think about what the gas has to push out of the way before its volume can be read from the scale.
For part (c), compare how readily carbon dioxide dissolves in water with how readily hydrogen does.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) A gas syringe measures the volume of gas and a stopwatch measures the time. The flask must be closed with a bung carrying a delivery tube that leads directly to the gas syringe, so that all the gas produced is collected and none escapes; the syringe reading is then taken at fixed times (for example every 10 s) from the moment the reactants are mixed. (b) Fill a measuring cylinder completely with water, invert it in a trough of water with its mouth below the water surface, and lead the delivery tube up into it. The gas collects at the top of the cylinder, pushing the water out, and its volume is read from the cylinder's scale. Before the reaction starts the cylinder must be completely full of water, with no trapped air, or every reading would be too large. (c) Carbon dioxide is fairly soluble in water, so some of the gas produced dissolves in the water instead of collecting at the top of the cylinder, and every volume read is smaller than the volume actually produced. Hydrogen is almost insoluble in water, so collecting hydrogen over water in this way works well.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
Naming the quantities first gives the apparatus straight away: a gas volume needs a gas syringe, and a time interval needs a stopwatch. What makes this a *rate* experiment rather than a single measurement is that the two are read together, so the flask must be sealed with a bung and delivery tube — any leak lets gas escape unmeasured and makes every later reading too small.

The alternative collects the gas over water: an inverted, completely water-filled measuring cylinder in a trough. The gas pushes water out of the cylinder and takes its place, so the volume of water displaced is the volume of gas collected. Any air left in the cylinder at the start would be counted as gas produced, so the cylinder must start full of water.

For $\mathrm{CaCO_3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$, the gas produced is carbon dioxide, which dissolves appreciably in water. Part of it therefore never reaches the top of the cylinder, so collection over water systematically underestimates the volume at every time. A gas syringe avoids the problem entirely because the gas never touches water. The same water-displacement method is perfectly good for a gas that barely dissolves, such as the hydrogen from $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$.
common_errors: Recording only one gas volume at the end of the reaction, which gives a single total and says nothing about how the rate changed with time.
Assuming that collecting a gas over water always works, without first checking whether that particular gas dissolves in water.

mcq.stem: A student needs to record the volume of gas produced during a reaction. Which apparatus should be used?

options.text: Measuring cylinder
options.why_wrong: a measuring cylinder used the normal way up is designed to measure a liquid poured into it and cannot trap an escaping gas (it only works for gas if filled with water and inverted in a trough); the gas syringe is the apparatus designed to collect and measure the gas directly.

options.text: Burette
options.why_wrong: a burette delivers a controlled volume of liquid through a tap; it is not used to collect or measure a gas.

options.text: Gas syringe
Volumetric pipette
options.why_wrong: a pipette delivers one single fixed volume of liquid; it has no way to collect a gas produced by a reaction.

mcq.explanation: A gas syringe is the only instrument listed that is designed to collect an escaping gas and read its volume directly from the plunger's position.

mcq.stem: Insoluble sand is filtered out of a sand–water mixture. Which statement correctly uses the terms 'residue' and 'filtrate'?

options.text: The sand on the filter paper is the filtrate; the water collected underneath is the residue.
options.why_wrong: this swaps the two terms: residue is what stays on the paper, filtrate is what passes through.

options.text: Both the sand and the water together are called the filtrate.
options.why_wrong: filtrate names only the liquid that passes through the paper, not the whole original mixture.

options.text: Neither term applies, because sand does not dissolve in water.
options.why_wrong: residue and filtrate describe what happens during filtration regardless of solubility; they do not require the solid to dissolve.

options.text: The sand on the filter paper is the residue; the water collected underneath is the filtrate.

mcq.explanation: Residue is defined as whatever is trapped on the filter paper (here, the sand); filtrate is defined as whatever passes through and is collected (here, the water).

mcq.stem: Which statement about a 'saturated solution' is correct?

options.text: A solution is saturated at a stated temperature if it cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
A solution is saturated whenever a large mass of solute has been dissolved in it, regardless of temperature.
options.why_wrong: this ignores temperature entirely, but how much solute can dissolve changes with temperature, so a mass alone cannot define saturation.

options.text: A solution stops being saturated as soon as it is allowed to cool down.
options.why_wrong: cooling usually reduces how much solute can stay dissolved, so a cooled solution can become even more saturated (or supersaturated), not less.

options.text: Only solutions containing visible undissolved solid, at any temperature, can be called saturated.
options.why_wrong: a solution exactly at its solubility limit, with no visible excess remaining, is also fully saturated — visible excess is one piece of evidence for saturation, not a requirement for the definition.

mcq.explanation: Saturation is defined relative to a stated temperature: once no more solute can dissolve at that specific temperature, the solution is saturated, whether or not solid happens to still be visibly undissolved.

mcq.stem: A burette and a measuring cylinder are both filled with the same liquid. Why is the burette the better choice for delivering a precisely controlled volume into a flask, drop by drop, until a colour changes?

options.text: The burette and the cylinder are equally suitable, since both display a volume scale.
options.why_wrong: a cylinder is read once, with no way to control or stop the flow of liquid partway through pouring, so it cannot deliver liquid dropwise to a chosen end point.

options.text: The burette has finer scale divisions and a tap, so a small, chosen volume can be released and stopped exactly when the colour change is seen.
The cylinder is actually more precise, because its scale covers a larger total volume.
options.why_wrong: covering a larger total volume with the same number of markings means coarser, not finer, divisions, so this makes the cylinder less precise, not more.

options.text: Neither instrument can be stopped partway through delivering liquid, so the choice does not matter.
options.why_wrong: a burette's tap is specifically designed to stop the flow at any instant, which is exactly what delivering liquid dropwise to an end point requires.

mcq.explanation: Only the burette combines fine (0.1 cm³) divisions with a tap that can be closed at any instant, which together allow liquid to be added a drop at a time and stopped exactly when the colour change appears.

flashcards.front: What are a solvent, a solute and a solution?
flashcards.back: Solvent: the liquid that does the dissolving. Solute: the substance that dissolves. Solution: the resulting mixture, in which the solute is no longer visible as separate particles.

flashcards.front: How does a burette differ from a measuring cylinder?
flashcards.back: A burette has fine (0.1 cm³) divisions and a tap, so a chosen volume can be released a drop at a time and stopped exactly; a measuring cylinder has coarse divisions and is simply read once, giving only an approximate volume.

flashcards.front: Why is 'this solution is saturated' an incomplete statement on its own?
flashcards.back: Solubility changes with temperature, so a solution can only be called saturated relative to a stated temperature; without a temperature, the claim cannot be checked.

flashcards.front: In filtration, what is the residue and what is the filtrate?
flashcards.back: Residue: whatever is trapped on the filter paper. Filtrate: whatever passes through the paper and is collected underneath.

flashcards.front: A reaction produces a gas that needs its volume measured. What apparatus is used, and why not a measuring cylinder?
flashcards.back: A gas syringe; a measuring cylinder used the normal way up holds a poured liquid and cannot trap an escaping gas (it can only be used if filled with water and inverted in a trough).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A measuring cylinder and a burette do the same job, because both are tubes marked with a volume scale, so either can be used whenever a 'precise volume' is needed.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both pieces of apparatus look similar (a graduated glass tube) and both measure liquid volume, so the difference in what each is actually for is easy to miss at a glance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner suggests reading a measuring cylinder drop by drop to deliver an exact volume, or claims a cylinder reading is just as reliable as a burette reading for a titration.
misconceptions.correct_model: A measuring cylinder has coarse divisions (often every 1 cm³) and is read once, giving an approximate volume; a burette has fine divisions (every 0.1 cm³) and a tap, so liquid can be released in small, controlled amounts and the volume delivered calculated precisely from two readings.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the division size on each instrument directly: count how many cm³ separate two neighbouring marks on a cylinder (coarse) against a burette (fine), then note that only the burette has a tap for controlled, dropwise delivery.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The word 'filtrate' names the solid caught on the filter paper after filtering a mixture.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both 'residue' and 'filtrate' are unfamiliar technical terms introduced together, so a learner may simply swap which word belongs to the solid and which belongs to the liquid.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels the liquid collected in the beaker as the 'residue', or labels the solid left on the paper as the 'filtrate'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Residue is whatever is left behind on the filter paper (usually an insoluble solid); filtrate is whatever passes through the paper and is collected underneath (a liquid, or a solution).
misconceptions.remediation: Trace the path of the mixture on a diagram: the solid stops at the paper (that is the residue), while the liquid continues down into the collecting vessel (that is the filtrate). Name each only after tracing where it actually ends up.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A solution counts as 'saturated' whenever it holds a large amount of dissolved solute, with some extra undissolved solid still visible at the bottom, regardless of temperature.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Visible undissolved solid is the easiest clue to notice, so a learner treats it as the whole definition and forgets that how much solute can dissolve depends on temperature.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calls a solution 'saturated' without stating a temperature, or assumes a saturated solution made while hot stays saturated once it has cooled.
misconceptions.correct_model: A saturated solution is one that cannot dissolve any more solute at a stated temperature, because solubility itself changes with temperature; 'saturated' with no temperature given is an incomplete statement.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask 'saturated at what temperature?' every time the word is used. Connect it to cooling: a solution saturated while hot usually cannot hold the same amount of dissolved solute once cooled, so extra solid comes out of solution.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing an instrument because it 'looks similar' to the right one (for example, using a measuring cylinder wherever a burette is needed).
common_mistakes.why: Several instruments share a graduated-tube appearance even though their precision and purpose are very different.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the exact physical quantity and the precision the task needs before choosing any apparatus.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swapping 'residue' and 'filtrate', or assuming each word always refers to the same one substance throughout an investigation.
common_mistakes.why: Both terms are introduced together and are defined by location in a single step, which is easy to forget once a procedure has several steps.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Trace exactly where the solid and the liquid each end up in the specific step being described, and re-check the terms at every new step.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a solution as 'saturated' without stating a temperature.
common_mistakes.why: The visible clue (undissolved solid) is noticed before the less visible condition (temperature) that the definition actually depends on.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always attach a temperature whenever the word 'saturated' is used.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a liquid-volume scale from above or below eye level instead of level with the meniscus.
common_mistakes.why: It feels natural to glance down at a scale on a bench rather than crouching to read it level with the liquid surface.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always lower your eye (or the apparatus) until your line of sight is level with the bottom of the meniscus before reading any volume scale.

exam_notes: Always name the instrument precisely (for example 'volumetric pipette', not just 'tube') — a vague answer can lose the mark even if the right idea is intended.
When asked to justify an apparatus choice, state the specific quantity being measured and the precision required, not just 'because it's more accurate'.
Whenever 'saturated' appears in an answer, check that a temperature is also stated; examiners often award a mark specifically for this.
When a question involves more than one step (for example filtration followed by evaporation), name the residue/filtrate of each step separately rather than giving one answer for the whole procedure.

summary.big_idea: Choosing the right instrument means matching it to the exact physical quantity and precision needed, not to how it looks; and 'residue'/'filtrate'/'saturated' are defined by role and by stated temperature, not by which substance is usually involved.
key_points: A balance measures mass, a thermometer measures temperature, a stopwatch measures time, and a gas syringe measures gas volume (a measuring cylinder only works for a gas if it is filled with water and inverted in a trough).
A measuring cylinder gives an approximate liquid volume; a pipette gives one fixed, accurate volume; a burette gives a variable, precisely controlled volume delivered through a tap.
Residue is whatever is trapped on filter paper; filtrate is whatever passes through — and a later step (like evaporation) can produce its own, new residue.
A solution is only correctly called 'saturated' when a temperature is stated alongside it, because solubility changes with temperature.
A substance that never dissolves (like sand or chalk in water) is never correctly called a solute, even when it is mixed into a liquid.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Name the quantity before the instrument, and name the step before using 'residue' or 'filtrate' or 'saturated'.

02_Acid-base_titration_as_measured_neutr.title: Acid-base titration as measured neutralisation
02_Acid-base_titration_as_measured_neutr.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe the burette/pipette/indicator setup for an acid-base titration, identify the end point from the specified colour change, and calculate the volume of solution delivered from a burette as the final reading minus the initial reading.

prerequisites.statement: Name and use the apparatus and solution vocabulary from the previous lesson, in particular that a burette delivers a variable, controlled volume and a pipette delivers one fixed volume (from an earlier lesson: apparatus and solution terms).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A titration is built entirely from the pipette and burette introduced in the previous lesson; without knowing what each one is for, the procedure's structure makes no sense.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that an acid and an alkali react together in a neutralisation reaction, and that an indicator changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline (from C07: acids, alkalis and indicators).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The end point of a titration is only detectable because the indicator's colour change signals the exact moment the solution stops being acidic (or alkaline) and becomes neutral; without this idea, the colour change has no meaning.

theory_blocks.title: Locating an exact point by controlled addition
theory_blocks.body:
A titration answers one question precisely: what volume of one solution, added to a known volume of another, is needed to reach neutralisation?

Because the reaction happens gradually as liquid is added, the only way to find that exact volume is to add the reagent in a controlled way and watch for a visible signal that marks the moment the reaction is complete.

The burette supplies [[blue:that controlled addition]]; the indicator supplies [[orange:the visible signal]]. Both roles depend on precise measurement, which is exactly why the previous lesson's apparatus choices matter here.

theory_blocks.title: The three roles: pipette, burette and indicator
theory_blocks.body:
| Apparatus | Role in the titration |
|---|---|
| Volumetric pipette | Transfers one fixed, known volume (for example 25.0 cm³) of one solution into the conical flask, once, before the titration begins. |
| Burette | Holds the second solution above the flask and releases it through a tap, a controlled amount at a time, while the total volume released is read from the scale. |
| Indicator | A few drops added to the flask; it changes colour at (or very close to) the point where the solution becomes neutral, giving a visible signal to stop adding liquid. |

The pipette's volume never changes between repeats of the titration: it is fixed by the pipette itself. The burette's volume is what varies and is what the experiment is actually trying to measure.

A **suitable indicator** for an acid-alkali titration is one that switches sharply between two clearly different colours over a very small added volume.

[[blue:**Methyl orange** is the usual choice: it is red in acid and yellow in alkali]], so a single drop past the end point changes the whole flask.

Litmus (red in acid, blue in alkali) correctly shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline, but its colour shifts too gradually through purple to pinpoint one exact volume, so it is not used for titrations.

theory_blocks.title: A safe, repeatable titration procedure
theory_blocks.body:
1. Rinse the pipette with the solution it will measure, then use it to transfer the fixed volume of that solution into a clean conical flask. Stand the flask on a **white tile**, so that the first faint colour change can be seen against a plain white background.
2. Add a few drops of a suitable indicator to the flask. **Methyl orange** is suitable for an acid-alkali titration: it is red in acid and yellow in alkali, and it switches between the two over a very small added volume.
3. Rinse the burette with a little of the solution it is about to hold (rinsing it with water instead would dilute that solution and make every titre too large). Fill the burette above the 0.00 cm³ mark, run a little through the tap to remove any air bubble from the jet below it, then record the starting (initial) reading.
4. Do a quick **rough titration** first: add the burette solution fairly quickly, swirling the flask constantly, and note the approximate volume at which the colour changes. This rough value is not used in the final result; it only tells you roughly where the end point lies.
5. Repeat with a fresh flask, now adding quickly up to about 2 cm³ before the rough value, then slow to a drop at a time, swirling constantly, watching closely for the first permanent colour change: this is the end point.
6. Record the final burette reading, and calculate the volume delivered as final reading minus initial reading.
7. Repeat steps 1-6 until at least two **concordant** results are obtained (results that agree with each other within 0.10 cm³), then use only the concordant results (never the rough titration) to find a mean volume delivered.

assets.caption: A burette's scale is numbered 0 at the top to 25 at the bottom. The shaded column is the solution in the burette at the initial reading; the lower red line marks the level at the end point, so the volume delivered is the difference between the two readings.
assets.purpose: Show, with the real geometry of a burette scale, that the delivered volume is a subtraction between two readings taken on the same instrument, not the final reading alone.

theory_blocks.title: Why a large excess damages the result
theory_blocks.body:
The end point is one specific volume: the volume at which the indicator's colour has just permanently changed.

Continuing to add reagent after that point does not make the result 'more certain' — [[red:it overshoots the true end point and makes the recorded final reading too large]], which makes the calculated delivered volume too large as well.

A titration is only useful if the recorded volume genuinely corresponds to the point of neutralisation; a result obtained by deliberately overshooting is not a safer measurement, it is a wrong one.

theory_blocks.title: Concordant results carry forward
theory_blocks.body:
The idea of repeating a measurement until results agree closely (concordant results), then averaging only the results that agree, is not unique to titration.

The same discipline reappears later in this unit: a melting point is trusted only once repeat measurements agree closely, and a qualitative test result is trusted only once the observation has been checked against the expected pattern,

not taken from a single uncertain reading.

keywords.definition: A technique that uses a controlled, measured addition of one solution to another to locate the exact volume needed for a reaction (such as neutralisation) to be complete.
The volume at which the indicator permanently changes colour, signalling that the reaction is complete.
Two or more titres that agree closely with each other, usually within 0.10 cm³, giving confidence in the mean value.
A quick, approximate first titration used only to estimate roughly where the end point lies, never included in the final mean.
The volume released from a burette during a titration, calculated as the final reading minus the initial reading.
An indicator suitable for acid-base titrations: red in acid and yellow in alkali, changing sharply between the two over a very small added volume.

worked_examples.statement: **Calculating a volume delivered.** During a titration, the burette's initial reading is 1.20 cm³. After the end point is reached, the final reading is 24.50 cm³. Calculate the volume of solution delivered.
knowns: Initial burette reading: 1.20 cm³
Final burette reading: 24.50 cm³
reasoning: The volume delivered is not the final reading alone; it is the change in reading caused by the tap being opened, which is final minus initial.
worked_examples.solution: Volume delivered $= 24.50 - 1.20 = 23.30\text{ cm}^3$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by addition: $1.20 + 23.30 = 24.50$, which matches the final reading, confirming the subtraction is consistent.

worked_examples.statement: **Using three titres to find a reliable volume.** Three accurate titrations give volumes delivered of 23.30 cm³, 23.25 cm³ and 23.35 cm³ (the rough titration result is not included). Are these results concordant? If so, calculate the mean volume to use as the final result.
knowns: Three accurate titres: 23.30, 23.25, 23.35 cm³
Concordant results agree within 0.10 cm³ of each other
reasoning: Find the spread of the three results: largest minus smallest $= 23.35 - 23.25 = 0.10\text{ cm}^3$.
This spread is exactly at the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit, so all three results are concordant with each other and all three can be used.
worked_examples.solution: Yes, the three titres are concordant (spread $=0.10$ cm³). Mean volume delivered $=23.30\text{ cm}^3$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Because all three results agree closely, none needs to be discarded as an outlier, and the mean is trustworthy as the final recorded titre.

worked_examples.statement: **Why overshooting ruins a titration.** A student, unsure exactly when the colour change happens, keeps adding the burette solution for several more seconds after the indicator first changes colour, 'to be safe'. The final reading is then 2.40 cm³ higher than it should have been. Explain the effect this has on the calculated volume delivered, and on the reliability of the result.
knowns: The student continued adding solution after the true end point
The final reading recorded is 2.40 cm³ too high
unknowns: Effect on the calculated volume delivered and on the result's reliability
reasoning: The volume delivered is calculated as final reading minus initial reading; since the final reading is 2.40 cm³ too high and the initial reading is unaffected, the calculated volume delivered is also exactly 2.40 cm³ too high.

This is not a 'safer' result: a titre that is too high will not agree with other, correctly stopped titres, so it will fail the concordance check (or, worse, falsely shift a mean if it is wrongly kept).
The error can only be fixed by repeating the titration and stopping precisely at the first permanent colour change, not by any calculation after the fact.
worked_examples.solution: The overshoot adds its full 2.40 cm³ error directly onto the calculated volume delivered, making the result too high and unreliable; it must be discarded and the titration repeated correctly, not corrected by calculation.
worked_examples.interpretation: A systematic overshoot cannot be 'averaged away' safely, because it is a result of a flawed procedure, not of ordinary small reading variation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Believing that adding extra reagent makes a result 'more definitely correct', when in fact it introduces a specific, repeatable error that makes the titre too large.

worked_examples.statement: **A full titration write-up.** A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of an alkali, measured by pipette, against an acid from a burette, using methyl orange as the indicator. The rough titration end point is at about 24 cm³. Two accurate titrations give: Titration 1, initial 0.40 cm³, final 24.15 cm³; Titration 2, initial 1.05 cm³, final 24.80 cm³. (a) Calculate the volume delivered in each accurate titration. (b) State whether the two results are concordant, with your reasoning. (c) Describe, in one sentence, what the student should observe at the end point.
knowns: Titration 1: initial 0.40 cm³, final 24.15 cm³
Titration 2: initial 1.05 cm³, final 24.80 cm³
Indicator: methyl orange, which is yellow in alkali and red in acid
reasoning: The spread between the two results is $23.75 - 23.75 = 0.00\text{ cm}^3$, which is well within the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit, so the results are concordant.

The flask starts alkaline, so the methyl orange in it is yellow; acid is added from the burette until the alkali is exactly neutralised, so the colour changes from yellow to orange-red at the end point.
worked_examples.solution:
(a) Both titrations deliver 23.75 cm³. (b) Yes, concordant: the two results are identical (spread 0.00 cm³, within the 0.10 cm³ limit).

(c) The methyl orange changes from yellow to orange-red at the end point, with a single extra drop making the new colour permanent.
worked_examples.interpretation: Identical accurate titres are the strongest possible evidence of a precise, repeatable titration, and confirm the final mean volume can be used with confidence.

guided_exercises.statement: A titration's burette readings are: initial 0.50 cm³, final 22.80 cm³. (a) Calculate the volume delivered. (b) Describe, in the correct order, the two steps that must happen before this titration even starts (involving the pipette and the indicator).
hints: For part (a), remember the volume delivered is always a subtraction, never the final reading by itself.
For part (b), think about what must be in the flask (a known volume of one solution, plus a visible signal) before any liquid is added from the burette.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) $22.80 - 0.50 = 22.30\text{ cm}^3$. (b) First, the pipette transfers a fixed, known volume of one solution into the conical flask; then a few drops of indicator are added to that flask, before any solution is added from the burette.
common_errors: Reporting 22.80 cm³ as the volume delivered, ignoring the initial reading of 0.50 cm³.

guided_exercises.statement: Put these titration steps into the correct order, and state which single step should never be included in the final mean of the accurate titres: (i) record the final burette reading; (ii) do a rough titration to estimate the end point; (iii) pipette the fixed volume of solution into the flask; (iv) add indicator to the flask; (v) record the initial burette reading; (vi) add solution dropwise near the expected end point, swirling constantly.
hints: The pipette's volume must be in the flask, with indicator added, before the burette is even read for the first time.
The rough titration happens before the accurate titrations and serves a different purpose from them.
guided_exercises.answer: First do a rough titration: (iii) pipette a fresh fixed volume into the flask, (iv) add indicator, (v) record the initial burette reading, add titrant while swirling and use (vi) dropwise addition near the end point, then (i) record the final reading. Repeat the same complete sequence with a fresh pipetted sample for every accurate titration. Do not include the rough titre in the final mean.
common_errors: Including the rough titration's volume in the final averaged result, which drags the mean away from the true, carefully measured end point.
guided_exercises.full_solution: First do a rough titration: (iii) pipette a fresh fixed volume into the flask, (iv) add indicator, (v) record the initial burette reading, add titrant while swirling and use (vi) dropwise addition near the end point, then (i) record the final reading. Repeat the same complete sequence with a fresh pipetted sample for every accurate titration. Do not include the rough titre in the final mean.

exercises.statement: A burette's initial reading is 2.30 cm³ and its final reading is 19.75 cm³. Calculate the volume delivered, and state the error a student would make by instead reporting 19.75 cm³ as the answer.
hints: Subtract the initial reading from the final reading.
Compare your correct answer with 19.75 cm³ to see the size of the error this mistake would cause.
exercises.answer: Volume delivered $= 19.75 - 2.30 = 17.45\text{ cm}^3$. Reporting 19.75 cm³ directly would overstate the volume delivered by 2.30 cm³, exactly the size of the ignored initial reading.
exercises.full_solution: $19.75 - 2.30 = 17.45\text{ cm}^3$. The error of reporting the final reading alone is always exactly equal to whatever the initial reading was, since that is precisely the amount being wrongly left out of the subtraction.
common_errors: Subtracting the readings in the wrong order (2.30 − 19.75), which gives a negative volume with no physical meaning.

exercises.statement: A student pipettes 25.0 cm³ of acid into a flask, then is told to repeat the exact same transfer for a second titration using 23.0 cm³ instead, 'to save time'. Explain what is wrong with this plan.
hints: Recall what a volumetric pipette is actually calibrated to do.
Compare this to what a measuring cylinder could or could not be asked to do instead.
exercises.answer: A volumetric pipette is calibrated to deliver only its one fixed, marked volume (25.0 cm³ here); it cannot be used to transfer a different, chosen volume such as 23.0 cm³. Every repeat of the titration must use the same 25.0 cm³ transferred by the pipette, so the burette volumes can be fairly compared between repeats.
exercises.full_solution: Changing the pipette's volume between repeats would also change how much of the first solution is being neutralised each time, so the volumes needed from the burette would no longer be comparable at all; the whole point of repeating a titration is to check that the *same* reaction, started from the *same* fixed volume, gives a consistent burette result.
common_errors: Treating the pipette as if it were a cylinder that can be filled to any chosen volume.

exercises.statement: Four titres are obtained: 18.40, 18.45, 18.90 and 18.35 cm³. One of these should be treated as an outlier and excluded before finding the mean. Identify it, justify your choice using the 0.10 cm³ concordance rule, and calculate the mean of the remaining three.
hints: Compare each titre with the others to see which one sits noticeably further away from the rest.
Once the outlier is excluded, check that the remaining three are mutually within 0.10 cm³ before averaging.
exercises.answer: 18.90 cm³ is the outlier (it is at least 0.45 cm³ away from each of the other three, far outside the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit). Mean of the remaining three $= (18.40+18.45+18.35) \div 3 = 55.20 \div 3 = 18.40\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.full_solution: Checking spreads: 18.40, 18.45 and 18.35 are mutually within 0.10 cm³ of each other (spread $=0.10$ cm³), so these three are concordant. 18.90 is at least 0.45 cm³ from every one of them, far exceeding the limit, so it is excluded. Mean of the kept values: $(18.40+18.45+18.35)\div3=55.20\div3=18.40\text{ cm}^3$.
common_errors: Averaging all four titres together, including the clear outlier, which drags the mean away from the true, concordant value.

exercises.statement: A technician in an unrelated investigation uses a burette to add a dye solution to a beaker, drop by drop, until a sensor detects a specific light absorbance, then records the initial and final burette readings. Explain, using the ideas from this lesson, how the technician should calculate the volume of dye added, and why running one 'rough' trial first would still be good practice here, even though this is not a titration between an acid and an alkali.
hints: The calculation for 'volume delivered from a burette' does not depend on what the two solutions actually are chemically.
A rough trial is useful whenever an unknown end point has to be located before the first accurate attempt.
exercises.answer: The volume of dye added is still the final burette reading minus the initial burette reading, exactly as in a titration, because this calculation only depends on how a burette works, not on what reaction (if any) is happening. A rough trial is still good practice here because it gives the technician an approximate idea of roughly how much dye is needed, so the accurate measurement can be approached slowly (drop by drop) only once the expected end point is close, instead of guessing blindly from the start.
exercises.full_solution: Nothing about the burette-reading subtraction or the logic of a rough-then-accurate approach depends specifically on acids, alkalis or indicators — both ideas transfer directly to any procedure that uses a burette to add a liquid until some observable signal (a colour change, a sensor reading, or anything else) is reached.
common_errors: Assuming the 'final minus initial' calculation or the rough-trial strategy only applies to acid-base titrations specifically.

exam_questions.statement: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution, added by pipette, against hydrochloric acid from a burette, using methyl orange as the indicator. (a) State the piece of apparatus that should be used to add exactly 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution to the flask, and explain why a measuring cylinder would not be suitable here. (b) The burette's initial reading is 0.80 cm³ and its final reading, at the end point, is 23.65 cm³. Calculate the volume of acid delivered. (c) Name the colour change the student should see at the end point.
hints: Part (a) should contrast the precision of the two instruments, not just name the correct one.
Part (b) is a straightforward subtraction, provided both readings are used; part (c) needs both colours, not just the colour at the end.
exam_questions.answer: (a) A volumetric pipette; a measuring cylinder's coarser divisions would not measure 25.0 cm³ precisely enough for a reliable titration result. (b) $23.65 - 0.80 = 22.85\text{ cm}^3$. (c) Methyl orange changes from yellow to orange-red at the end point.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The pipette is calibrated specifically to deliver 25.0 cm³ accurately and repeatably; a measuring cylinder's coarse 1 cm³ divisions would introduce far more uncertainty into the starting volume, which would then affect every subsequent titre. (b) $23.65-0.80=22.85$ cm³, found by subtracting the initial reading from the final reading. (c) The flask starts alkaline, so the methyl orange in it is yellow; acid is added until the sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised, so the colour changes from yellow to orange-red. A white tile under the flask gives a plain background against which that first permanent colour change can be seen (swirling the flask constantly also helps, by mixing each drop in before the next is added).
mark_scheme: Pipette correctly named in part (a) (1 mark).
Reason in part (a) refers to precision/accuracy of the volume transferred, not just 'it's more accurate' with no explanation (1 mark).
Correct subtraction $23.65-0.80=22.85$ cm³ in part (b) (1 mark).
Correct colour change named in part (c) — yellow to orange-red (yellow to red accepted) (1 mark).
common_errors: Naming the correct apparatus in part (a) but giving no reason beyond 'it is more accurate', without referring to the specific precision comparison; or giving only the final colour in part (c) instead of the change from one colour to the other.

exam_questions.statement: Three accurate titrations give volumes delivered of 15.20 cm³, 15.65 cm³ and 15.25 cm³. (a) Identify which result should be treated with suspicion, giving a numerical reason. (b) Calculate a suitable mean titre using only the results you judge to be concordant. (c) A student suggests simply repeating the titration many more times and averaging all the results together, including the suspicious one, to 'cancel out the error'. Explain why this is not good practice.
hints: Compare each pair of results against the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit before deciding which to keep.
Part (c) should explain what kind of error an outlier usually represents, not just restate the concordance rule.
exam_questions.answer: (a) 15.65 cm³ is suspicious: it differs from both other results by about 0.40-0.45 cm³, far outside the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit. (b) Mean of the concordant pair $=(15.20+15.25)\div2=15.225$, which is given as $15.23\text{ cm}^3$ (15.225 cm³ is also acceptable). (c) The suspicious result is an anomalous result caused by a mistake in that particular run (such as overshooting the end point), not a small random variation; averaging it in does not cancel the error out, it simply drags the mean away from the true value. Anomalous results should be identified and left out (and the titration repeated), not averaged in.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) 15.20 and 15.25 differ by only 0.05 cm³ (concordant); 15.65 differs from 15.20 by 0.45 cm³ and from 15.25 by 0.40 cm³, both far outside 0.10 cm³. (b) Using only 15.20 and 15.25: mean $=15.225 \approx 15.23\text{ cm}^3$. (c) Small random variations in reading tend to average out over repeats, but a titre affected by a specific procedural mistake (like overshooting) is an anomalous result that is always wrong in one direction, so including it biases the mean however many other results are added — the anomalous result must be identified and excluded instead.
mark_scheme: 15.65 cm³ correctly identified as the outlier, with a numerical comparison shown (1 mark).
Correct mean of the two concordant results, with working shown (1 mark).

Explanation in part (c) states that the suspicious titre is an anomalous result caused by a mistake (not random variation) (1 mark), so including it biases the mean and it should be excluded/repeated instead (1 mark).
common_errors: Averaging all three titres together in part (b) instead of excluding the outlier first.

challenge_questions.statement: **Three results that agree, and are all wrong.** A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of an alkali against an acid from a burette and records three titres: 24.90 cm³, 24.95 cm³ and 24.85 cm³. Before filling the burette, the student rinsed it out with distilled water and nothing else. (a) Show that the three titres are concordant, and calculate the mean titre. (b) Explain why all three results are nevertheless wrong, and state clearly whether they are too large or too small. (c) State the single change to the procedure that would remove this error, and explain why repeating the titration ten more times would not.
hints: For part (a), compare the largest and smallest titres against the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit.
For part (b), think about what is left clinging to the inside of a burette that has just been rinsed with water, and what it does to the acid poured in afterwards.
For part (c), ask whether the fault happens differently each time or in exactly the same way every time.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Spread $= 24.95 - 24.85 = 0.10\text{ cm}^3$, which is within the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit, so the three titres are concordant. Mean $= (24.90 + 24.95 + 24.85) \div 3 = 74.70 \div 3 = 24.90\text{ cm}^3$. (b) Rinsing the burette with distilled water leaves a film of water inside it, which slightly dilutes the acid poured in afterwards. Each cm³ of that diluted acid contains less acid than it should, so a larger volume has to be run out to neutralise the same fixed 25.0 cm³ of alkali: all three titres are too large. (c) Rinse the burette with a little of the acid it is about to hold (and discard that rinsing) instead of with water. Repeating the titration would not help, because the same fault is made in exactly the same way every time, shifting every titre in the same direction by about the same amount; that is a systematic error, and averaging more results that all carry it simply gives a more precise version of the same wrong value.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
(a) Largest minus smallest is $24.95-24.85=0.10\text{ cm}^3$, exactly at the 0.10 cm³ limit, so the set counts as concordant; the mean is $74.70\div3=24.90\text{ cm}^3$.

(b) The water left behind after rinsing mixes with the acid that is poured in, so the acid actually delivered from the burette is slightly more dilute than the acid in the bottle. More of it is therefore needed to neutralise the fixed volume of alkali in the flask, and every titre comes out too large.

(c) The cure is to rinse the burette with the acid it will hold, so that anything left clinging inside is that same acid rather than water. Concordance only shows that the three results scatter very little — it measures precision, not accuracy. A fault built into the method shifts every result the same way, so it survives any number of repeats; only changing the method removes it.
common_errors: Treating concordant results as proof that the answer is correct, when concordance only shows the repeats agree with each other.
Arguing that the diluted acid makes the titre smaller, by confusing 'weaker acid' with 'less acid needed'.

mcq.stem: A burette's initial reading is 3.40 cm³ and its final reading is 27.90 cm³. What volume was delivered?

options.why_wrong: this is the final reading alone, with the initial reading of 3.40 cm³ not subtracted.
this comes from adding the two readings together instead of subtracting them.

options.text: 3.40 cm³
options.why_wrong: this is only the initial reading, not the volume actually delivered during the titration.

mcq.explanation: Volume delivered $= 27.90 - 3.40 = 24.50\text{ cm}^3$: always the final reading minus the initial reading.

mcq.stem: Which statement about the volumetric pipette used in a titration is correct?

options.text: It can be filled to any volume the student chooses, like a measuring cylinder.
options.why_wrong: a volumetric pipette is calibrated to one single marked volume; it is not adjustable like a measuring cylinder.

options.text: It is used continuously throughout the titration, alongside the burette.
options.why_wrong: the pipette's one transfer happens before the titration starts; only the burette is used throughout the titration itself.

options.text: Its volume changes between repeat titrations to help locate the end point.
options.why_wrong: the pipette's volume is fixed and identical in every repeat; only the burette volume changes as the end point is located.

options.text: It delivers the same fixed volume every time it is used, and is used once, before the burette additions begin.

mcq.explanation: A volumetric pipette is calibrated to one single, fixed volume and is used once, before any burette solution is added, to transfer a known starting volume into the flask.

mcq.stem: Why is deliberately adding a large excess of the burette solution, well past the first colour change, a poor way to 'make sure' the end point has been reached?

options.text: It overshoots the true end point, making the recorded volume too large and the result inaccurate.
It has no effect on the result, since the indicator's colour cannot change any further anyway.
options.why_wrong: the harmful effect is not on the indicator's colour but on the recorded burette volume, which becomes too large once the true end point has already passed.

options.text: It only wastes time, but the calculated volume delivered is unaffected.
options.why_wrong: continuing to add solution after the true end point directly increases the final burette reading, so the calculated volume delivered is affected, not unaffected.

options.text: It is actually good practice, since more reagent means a more reliable result.
options.why_wrong: the reliability of a titration depends on stopping at the correct volume, not on adding as much reagent as possible.

mcq.explanation: The end point is one specific volume; continuing past it increases the final reading (and therefore the calculated volume delivered) beyond the true value, making the result too large, not more reliable.

mcq.stem: Three accurate titres are 21.10, 21.15 and 21.60 cm³. Using the 0.10 cm³ concordance rule, which titre should be excluded before averaging?

options.why_wrong: 21.10 cm³ is within 0.05 cm³ of 21.15 cm³, well inside the concordance limit, so it should be kept, not excluded.
21.15 cm³ is within 0.05 cm³ of 21.10 cm³, well inside the concordance limit, so it should be kept, not excluded.

options.text: None of them; all three should be averaged together.
options.why_wrong: 21.60 cm³ differs from the other two by at least 0.45 cm³, far outside the 0.10 cm³ concordance limit, so it cannot be included without checking it separately.

mcq.explanation: 21.10 and 21.15 cm³ differ by only 0.05 cm³ (concordant); 21.60 cm³ differs from both by at least 0.45 cm³, well outside the 0.10 cm³ limit, so it is the one excluded.

flashcards.front: How is the volume delivered from a burette calculated?
flashcards.back: Volume delivered = final burette reading − initial burette reading.

flashcards.front: How does the pipette's role in a titration differ from the burette's role?
flashcards.back: The pipette delivers one fixed volume, once, before the titration starts. The burette delivers a variable, controlled volume throughout the titration, and its reading is what is actually measured.

flashcards.front: Why is adding a large excess past the colour change not a 'safer' titration result?
flashcards.back: It overshoots the true end point, making the final reading (and so the calculated volume delivered) too large; the result becomes less accurate, not more reliable.

flashcards.front: What does it mean for two titres to be 'concordant'?
flashcards.back: They agree closely with each other, usually within 0.10 cm³, which gives confidence that both are close to the true end-point volume.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of the 'rough' titration done first?
