Propanone and ethanol are miscible liquids with different boiling points and both evaporate, so a fractionating column is needed; the dissolved solid is non-volatile, so it never evaporates and is simply left behind in the flask. Heat the mixture gently with the thermometer bulb level with the side-arm. Start collecting when the thermometer steadies at about 56 °C, and change the receiver as soon as the reading begins to climb towards 78 °C, because ethanol is then distilling over as well. (b) Measure the boiling point of the collected liquid: a sharp, reproducible boiling point at 56 °C supports the conclusion that it is pure propanone, whereas a range spread over several degrees, or a value above 56 °C, would show that ethanol is still present.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Each feature of the mixture is matched to what it forces you to do. The non-volatile solid does not evaporate, so it needs no separate step at all — distillation leaves it in the flask. The two liquids, however, both evaporate, so a single evaporation and condensation (simple distillation) would collect a vapour still containing both; only the repeated evaporation-condensation cycles of a packed fractionating column enrich the rising vapour enough in the lower-boiling propanone for a clean fraction to be collected. The thermometer is the instrument that tells you which liquid is coming over, which is why its bulb must be level with the side-arm and why a steady reading, rather than a rising one, marks the propanone fraction. Finally, the boiling-point check in (b) is the same purity evidence used later in this lesson: a sharp value matching the reference is strong evidence, not unchallengeable proof, so an independent test such as chromatography would make the conclusion stronger still.
common_errors: Choosing simple distillation because the two boiling points look far apart; propanone and ethanol mix with each other, so a fractionating column is needed to separate them.

mcq.stem: Which statement about filtration is correct?

options.text: It can separate any two substances mixed together, solid or liquid.
options.why_wrong: filtration relies specifically on a solid being too large to pass through the paper's pores; it has no way to separate two liquids mixed at a molecular level.

options.text: It works equally well on a mixture of two miscible liquids as on a solid-liquid mixture.
options.why_wrong: two miscible liquids have no solid particles for the filter paper to trap, so filtration cannot separate them at all.

options.text: It can only separate an insoluble solid from a liquid; it cannot separate two miscible liquids.
It separates liquids by their different boiling points.
options.why_wrong: separating liquids by boiling point is what distillation does, not filtration, which relies on particle size, not boiling point.

mcq.explanation: Filtration depends entirely on one component being an insoluble solid, large enough to be physically trapped by the filter paper's pores; it has no mechanism for separating two miscible liquids.

mcq.stem: What is the correct product recovered from crystallisation?

options.text: A pure liquid, collected after condensing it in a condenser.
options.why_wrong: collecting a condensed pure liquid describes distillation, not crystallisation, which has no condenser and produces a solid product.

options.text: Both a pure solid and a pure liquid in equal amounts.
options.why_wrong: the leftover mother liquor still contains dissolved impurities and is not a purified product; only the solid crystals are the technique's intended, purified product.

options.text: The original solvent, now free of any dissolved solute.
options.why_wrong: the solvent that remains (the mother liquor) still carries dissolved solute and impurities; crystallisation does not purify the solvent itself.

options.text: A pure solid (the dissolved solute), leaving the mother liquor behind.

mcq.explanation: Crystallisation evaporates and cools a solution until the dissolved solute comes out of solution as solid crystals; the remaining mother liquor is not a purified product.

mcq.stem: A sample's boiling point exactly matches a reference value for substance M. What is the most accurate conclusion?

options.text: This is strong evidence that the sample is pure M, but not absolute, unchallengeable proof on its own.
This proves with complete certainty that the sample is pure M.
options.why_wrong: a different substance could, in principle, happen to share a very similar or identical boiling point, so a single matching value cannot give absolute certainty on its own.

options.text: Boiling point data cannot be used as purity evidence at all.
options.why_wrong: a sharp, matching boiling point is genuinely useful, strong evidence for purity and identity; it is simply not a complete, unchallengeable proof by itself.

options.text: The result is meaningless unless the sample's mass is also known.
options.why_wrong: the mass of the sample does not affect its boiling point or what the comparison to a reference value shows about its purity.

mcq.explanation: A matching boiling point is strong supporting evidence, but because another substance could coincidentally share a similar value, it is not an absolute, unchallengeable proof on its own.

mcq.stem: Two liquids that mix completely with each other have boiling points of 70 °C and 92 °C. Which technique should be used to separate them from each other?

options.text: Simple distillation, because the two boiling points are 22 °C apart.
options.why_wrong: simple distillation is used to get a liquid out of a solution, where the dissolved solid does not evaporate; here both components are liquids that evaporate, so a single evaporation would still collect a mixture.

options.text: Fractional distillation, because the mixture is two miscible liquids with different boiling points.
Filtration, since both substances are liquids.
options.why_wrong: filtration requires an insoluble solid to trap; it has no way to separate two liquids at all, regardless of their boiling points.

options.text: Crystallisation, since the mixture contains two components.
options.why_wrong: crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid from a solution; it is not used on a mixture of two liquids at all.

mcq.explanation: Both components evaporate, so one evaporation and condensation would collect a mixture again; the repeated cycles inside a fractionating column are needed, all the more so because the gap is only $92-70=22\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

flashcards.front: How does crystallisation's product differ from simple distillation's product?
flashcards.back: Crystallisation recovers a pure solid (the dissolved solute); simple distillation recovers a pure liquid (the distillate), leaving any dissolved solid behind in the flask.

flashcards.front: Can filtration separate a mixture of two miscible liquids?
flashcards.back: No. Filtration only traps an insoluble solid; two miscible liquids have no solid particles for the paper to catch, so a boiling-point-based technique (distillation) is needed instead.

flashcards.front: When is fractional distillation needed instead of simple distillation?
flashcards.back: When the mixture is two or more miscible liquids with different boiling points, since both of them evaporate. Simple distillation is for getting a liquid out of a solution, where the dissolved solid does not evaporate at all.

flashcards.front: What does 'using a suitable solvent' mean as a separation method?
flashcards.back: Choosing a solvent that dissolves one component of a mixture but not the other, so that filtration can then separate them and crystallisation (or evaporation) recovers the dissolved component as a solid.

flashcards.front: What two features of a melting-point result suggest a sample is impure?
flashcards.back: A broad (not sharp) melting range, and a range shifted away from (typically below) the pure reference value.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Filtration can separate a mixture of two liquids that are completely mixed together (miscible), such as ethanol and water.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Filtration is the first separation technique learned, so it can be over-generalised to 'the' method for separating any mixture, not just a solid from a liquid.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner suggests filtering a mixture of two miscible liquids, or expects filter paper to trap one liquid while letting the other through.
misconceptions.correct_model: Filtration only works when one component is an insoluble solid, large enough to be physically trapped by the tiny pores in the filter paper. Two miscible liquids are mixed at a molecular level with nothing solid to trap, so filtration cannot separate them at all; a difference in boiling point (distillation) is needed instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what, physically, the filter paper's pores could possibly catch in a liquid-liquid mixture; since there are no solid particles present, there is nothing for the paper to trap.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Crystallisation produces a pure liquid, in the same way that distillation does.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both techniques start from a solution and both are used to 'purify' something, so the type of pure product each one gives (solid versus liquid) can be blurred together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes crystallisation as collecting a pure liquid, or expects the leftover liquid after crystallisation (the mother liquor) to be pure solvent.
misconceptions.correct_model: Crystallisation recovers a pure **solid** (the dissolved solute) from a solution, by evaporating enough solvent (or cooling) until the solute comes out of solution as crystals. The remaining liquid, called the mother liquor, still contains dissolved impurities and is not purified by this process; only distillation collects a purified liquid.
misconceptions.remediation: Name the product of each technique explicitly: crystallisation's useful product is the solid crystals; distillation's useful product is the condensed liquid (distillate). Ask which one the technique is even designed to collect.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A measured melting or boiling point, on its own, identifies a substance with complete certainty, however close it is to a reference value.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A melting/boiling point feels like a precise, 'fixed' number, so matching it to a table value can feel like a conclusive identification.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner concludes a substance's identity from a single matching melting/boiling point without considering that another substance could share, or nearly share, the same value.
misconceptions.correct_model: A sharp melting/boiling point matching a reference value is strong evidence supporting both purity and identity, but it is not absolute proof: different substances can occasionally have very similar melting or boiling points. As with chromatography, this evidence is strongest when combined with another independent method.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask whether any other known substance could plausibly share this same melting/boiling point, and whether a second, independent test (for example chromatography, or a different physical or chemical property) has been used to confirm the identification.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to filter a mixture of two miscible liquids.
common_mistakes.why: Filtration is the first separation technique learned, so it can be over-applied to any mixture.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check first whether an insoluble solid is actually present; filtration has no mechanism for separating two liquids mixed at a molecular level.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting crystallisation to produce a pure liquid.
common_mistakes.why: Both crystallisation and distillation start from a solution and are used to 'purify' something.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the product each technique is designed to give: crystallisation gives a solid; distillation gives a liquid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing simple distillation to separate two liquids that mix with each other.
common_mistakes.why: Simple distillation is the more familiar, 'default' form of distillation, and a large boiling-point gap can make it look sufficient.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask what is being separated from what: a liquid out of a solution needs simple distillation, while liquids that mix with each other need a fractionating column.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a single matching melting or boiling point as absolute proof of identity.
common_mistakes.why: A precise numerical match feels conclusive on its own.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State the result as strong supporting evidence, and look for a second, independent test (such as chromatography) to confirm it.

exam_notes: Always name the property the chosen technique relies on (solubility, particle size, or boiling-point difference), not just the technique's name, since the reasoning is often worth its own mark.
Before naming a distillation, say what kind of mixture it is: a liquid out of a solution needs simple distillation, while liquids that mix with each other need fractional distillation.
When assessing purity from a melting or boiling point, comment on both the sharpness (width) of the range and its position relative to the reference value.
When a question asks for an additional test to support an identification, name a genuinely different method (such as chromatography), not a repeat of the same measurement.

summary.big_idea: Choosing a separation technique means identifying the one physical property (particle size, solubility, or boiling-point difference) that actually distinguishes the mixture's components, and a sharp phase point matching a reference value is strong, but not absolute, evidence of purity and identity.
key_points: Filtration only works on an insoluble solid trapped by filter paper; it cannot separate two miscible liquids.
Crystallisation recovers a pure solid; simple distillation recovers a pure liquid; they are not interchangeable despite both starting from a solution.
Simple distillation gets a liquid out of a solution, because the dissolved solid does not evaporate; fractional distillation's packed column is needed to separate liquids that mix with each other.
A suitable solvent is one that dissolves one component of a mixture and not the other, so filtration can then separate them and crystallisation recovers the dissolved solid.
A sharp, matching melting or boiling point is strong purity/identity evidence, not absolute proof; a broad or shifted range suggests impurity.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Name the property that differs before naming the technique, and treat a matching phase point as strong evidence, never as unchallengeable proof on its own.

05_Identifying_anions_and_gases.json.title: Identifying anions and gases
05_Identifying_anions_and_gases.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe the tests for carbonate, halide (chloride, bromide, iodide), nitrate and sulfate ions, stating the exact reagent, any required acidification, and the resulting precipitate or gas observed.
Describe the tests used to identify ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen and oxygen gases, stating the reagent or action, and the resulting observation.

prerequisites.statement: Use the terms solution and precipitate to describe what happens when two solutions are mixed (from an earlier lesson: solution terms).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every anion test in this lesson is reported as a reagent added to a solution producing either a precipitate or a gas; without this vocabulary, the test results cannot be described precisely.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that an acid reacts with a base or a carbonate, and that salts are formed from acid-base and acid-carbonate reactions (from the acids and salts unit).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several anion tests work by first adding an acid; without already knowing what an acid does to a carbonate, or why an acid is added before a precipitating reagent, the purpose of acidification cannot be understood, only memorised.

theory_blocks.title: A qualitative test is three linked steps, not one observation
theory_blocks.body:
Identifying an ion or a gas is never just 'what did you see?'. A valid qualitative test is always a chain of three linked parts: the [[blue:**reagent or action**]] used, the [[orange:**observation**]] that results, and the [[green:**inference**]] that observation supports.

Reporting only the observation ('a white precipitate formed') without the reagent that produced it is not enough information to draw any conclusion at all, because several different reagents can give the same-looking result.

Every test in this lesson should be learned, and reported, as all three parts together.

theory_blocks.title: Anion tests: reagent, acidification and result
theory_blocks.body:
| Ion tested | Reagent / action | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Carbonate ($\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}$) | Add dilute acid. | Effervescence (bubbles); the gas produced turns limewater milky, confirming carbon dioxide. |
| Chloride ($\mathrm{Cl^-}$) | Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. | White precipitate. |
| Bromide ($\mathrm{Br^-}$) | Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. | Cream precipitate. |
| Iodide ($\mathrm{I^-}$) | Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. | Yellow precipitate. |
| Sulfate ($\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$) | Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate. | White precipitate. |
| Nitrate ($\mathrm{NO_{3}^-}$) | Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and a small piece of aluminium foil, then warm gently. | Ammonia gas is released (detected by its smell and by turning damp red litmus paper blue). |

Notice that chloride and sulfate both give a white precipitate: the colour alone never distinguishes them. Only the specific reagent (silver nitrate versus barium nitrate) tied to that white precipitate identifies which ion is actually present.

theory_blocks.title: Why acidify first?
theory_blocks.body:
Carbonate ions, if present in a sample, would themselves react with silver nitrate or with barium nitrate to form a precipitate — not because a halide or sulfate is present, but simply because carbonate reacts with these reagents too.

Adding dilute acid *before* the test reagent reacts with (and removes) any carbonate present, releasing it as carbon dioxide gas, so that any precipitate observed afterwards can only be explained by the ion actually being tested for.

Skipping this step risks a **false positive**: a precipitate that looks exactly like a correct result but is actually caused by an entirely different ion that was never ruled out.

theory_blocks.title: Gas tests
theory_blocks.body:
| Gas | Test | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_{2}}$) | Bubble the gas through limewater. | The limewater turns milky (cloudy). |
| Ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_{3}}$) | Hold damp red litmus paper in the gas. | The litmus paper turns blue. |
| Chlorine ($\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$) | Hold damp litmus paper in the gas. | The litmus paper is bleached (turns white). |
| Hydrogen ($\mathrm{H_{2}}$) | Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the test tube. | A squeaky 'pop' is heard as the hydrogen itself burns rapidly. |
| Oxygen ($\mathrm{O_{2}}$) | Hold a glowing splint in the gas. | The splint relights, bursting back into flame. |

The hydrogen and oxygen tests look superficially similar (both use a splint) but check for opposite things: the pop test checks whether the gas itself is flammable; the relighting test checks whether the gas supports something else's combustion.

assets.caption: Testing a gas with limewater. The reaction tube is upright and closed with a bung; the delivery tube carries the gas produced over and down into a second, upright test tube, ending below the surface of the limewater. The limewater turning milky (cloudy) shows that the gas is carbon dioxide.
assets.purpose: Show the physical apparatus behind the carbon dioxide/limewater test, drawn correctly: upright test tubes, a bung in the reaction tube, and a delivery tube that dips below the limewater surface so the gas has to bubble through it. The same delivery-tube set-up is reused (with a splint or damp litmus paper instead of limewater) for the other gas tests in this lesson.

theory_blocks.title: State the reagent, not just the colour
theory_blocks.body:
Because chloride and sulfate both give a white precipitate, and because several other combinations of ion and reagent can coincidentally look similar, a reported observation is only useful evidence when the reagent (and any acidification) is stated alongside it.

[[red:'A white precipitate formed' is an incomplete, ambiguous statement]]; 'a white precipitate formed on adding acidified silver nitrate' is a complete, usable piece of evidence.

theory_blocks.title: The same chain, one ion family at a time
theory_blocks.body:
This lesson's reagent-observation-inference chain is exactly the structure the next lesson uses for cation tests, just applied to a different family of ions (metal cations, identified with sodium hydroxide, ammonia and flame tests, rather than anions identified with acidification and precipitating reagents).

The discipline of always stating the full chain, and never trusting a single observation on its own, carries forward unchanged.

keywords.definition: An insoluble solid that forms and separates out when two solutions are mixed.
Adding a dilute acid before a test reagent, to remove interference from carbonate ions that would otherwise give a false positive.
Bubbling caused by a gas being released from a reaction, such as a carbonate reacting with an acid.
A test result that appears to confirm an ion is present when it is not, usually because an untested interfering substance produced the same observation.
A solution that turns milky (cloudy) in the presence of carbon dioxide gas, used as the standard test for that gas.

worked_examples.statement: **A first carbonate test.** A white solid is suspected to be a carbonate. Describe the test, including the full reagent-observation-inference chain.
knowns: Suspected ion: carbonate
Reagent for carbonate: dilute acid
reasoning: Add dilute acid to the solid: this is the reagent/action step.
Effervescence (bubbling) is observed, and the gas produced turns limewater milky: this is the observation step.
A gas that turns limewater milky is confirmed as carbon dioxide, which is consistent with the original solid being a carbonate: this is the inference step.
worked_examples.solution: Add dilute acid to the solid. Effervescence occurs, and the gas produced turns limewater milky, confirming carbon dioxide and supporting that the original solid is a carbonate.
worked_examples.interpretation: All three parts (reagent, observation, inference) are stated explicitly, rather than jumping straight from 'bubbles' to 'it's a carbonate' without confirming the gas.

worked_examples.statement: **A full halide test, with acidification.** A solution is suspected to contain chloride ions, but carbonate ions might also be present. Describe a test that correctly identifies chloride without being misled by the carbonate.
knowns: Suspected ion: chloride
Possible interference: carbonate ions
unknowns: A test that avoids a false positive from carbonate
reasoning: Carbonate ions would also form a precipitate with silver nitrate directly, so adding silver nitrate straight away could give a misleading positive result even without chloride present.
Acidifying the solution with dilute nitric acid first reacts away any carbonate present (releasing it as carbon dioxide gas), removing that source of interference.
Only then is silver nitrate solution added; a white precipitate at this stage can only be explained by chloride, since the carbonate interference has already been ruled out.
worked_examples.solution: Acidify the solution with dilute nitric acid first, then add silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate confirms chloride, with the acidification step having already ruled out carbonate as an alternative explanation.
worked_examples.interpretation: The acidification step is not a formality; it is what makes the final white precipitate unambiguous evidence for chloride specifically.

worked_examples.statement: **Discriminating two similar-looking results.** Two unlabelled test tubes both show a white precipitate after a reagent was added. Test tube 1 had acidified silver nitrate added; test tube 2 had acidified barium nitrate added. Explain what each result shows, and why the colour alone could not have told them apart.
knowns: Test tube 1: acidified silver nitrate added, white precipitate
Test tube 2: acidified barium nitrate added, white precipitate
reasoning: Test tube 1's reagent (acidified silver nitrate) is specifically the chloride test, so its white precipitate indicates chloride ions.
Test tube 2's reagent (acidified barium nitrate) is specifically the sulfate test, so its white precipitate indicates sulfate ions, a completely different ion.

If only the colour ('white precipitate') had been reported for each, without naming the reagent used, the two results would have looked identical on paper despite indicating two entirely different ions.
worked_examples.solution:
Test tube 1 (acidified silver nitrate, white precipitate): chloride ions present. Test tube 2 (acidified barium nitrate, white precipitate): sulfate ions present.

The colour alone cannot distinguish them; only the reagent used, stated alongside the colour, makes the evidence usable.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the clearest possible demonstration that 'white precipitate' is not, by itself, a complete piece of evidence for any one ion.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding both test tubes contain the same ion because both show the same precipitate colour, without checking which reagent produced each one.

worked_examples.statement: **A two-stage unknown identification.** An unknown solid is tested. Test 1: dilute acid is added and effervescence is observed; the gas produced turns limewater milky. Test 2: a separate sample of the solid is dissolved in water, acidified with dilute nitric acid, and silver nitrate solution is added; no precipitate forms. (a) What does Test 1 show? (b) What does Test 2 show, and why was acidification included even though the final result is negative? (c) What class of substance is the solid most likely to be, based on both tests together?
knowns: Test 1: effervescence; gas turns limewater milky
Test 2: acidified silver nitrate added, no precipitate
unknowns: Interpretation of each test, and overall conclusion
reasoning: (a) Effervescence with a gas that turns limewater milky is the carbonate test's positive result, showing the solid is very likely a carbonate.

(b) No precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows chloride, bromide and iodide ions are all absent.

Acidification was essential here, because Test 1 shows the solid contains carbonate: without dilute nitric acid, the carbonate ions would react with silver nitrate to form a precipitate, which could be mistaken for a halide result.

Adding the acid first removes the carbonate (as carbon dioxide), so the 'no precipitate' result can be trusted.
(c) Combining both tests: the solid is a carbonate, and specifically not a chloride, bromide or iodide salt.
worked_examples.interpretation: Combining a positive result from one test with a negative result from another narrows down the possible identity of the solid far more precisely than either test alone.

guided_exercises.statement: Complete the full reagent-observation-inference chain for testing a solution suspected to contain sulfate ions.
hints: Recall which acid is used to acidify before the sulfate test (the same acid as in the halide test), and why an acid that already contains sulfate ions must not be used.
State the reagent added after acidification, and the expected precipitate colour.
guided_exercises.answer: Acidify the solution with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate. A white precipitate confirms sulfate ions.
common_errors: Acidifying with dilute sulfuric acid, which itself adds sulfate ions and so gives a white precipitate with barium nitrate whatever the sample contains (a false positive).

guided_exercises.statement: A test tube of gas is tested twice: first with a lighted splint, producing a squeaky pop, and second (a fresh sample) with a glowing splint, which does not relight. Identify the gas, explaining both results.
hints: Recall which gas specifically produces a 'pop' with a lighted splint.
Check that a glowing splint not relighting is consistent with your answer, rather than contradicting it.
guided_exercises.answer: The gas is hydrogen. The pop with a lighted splint is hydrogen's characteristic test, confirming hydrogen; a glowing splint not relighting is consistent with this, since relighting a glowing splint is the separate test for oxygen, not hydrogen.
common_errors: Confusing the two tests and concluding the gas is oxygen because a splint was involved, without checking which specific splint state (lit or glowing) matched which result.

exercises.statement: State the reagent, observation and inference for testing a solution suspected to contain bromide ions.
hints: Recall which acid is used before the halide test, and which reagent is added after it.
Recall the specific precipitate colour for bromide, which is different from chloride's.
exercises.answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. A cream precipitate confirms bromide ions.
exercises.full_solution: The halide test procedure (acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate) is the same for chloride, bromide and iodide; only the resulting precipitate colour differs between them, with bromide giving a cream precipitate specifically.
common_errors: Reporting a white precipitate (chloride's colour) instead of the correct cream precipitate for bromide.

exercises.statement: A gas is bubbled through limewater and the limewater turns milky. A second, unrelated sample of gas is tested with damp litmus paper and the paper is bleached white. Identify each gas.
hints: Match each described observation to exactly one gas test from this lesson's table.
Check that no other gas in the table shares either observation.
exercises.answer: First gas: carbon dioxide (limewater turns milky). Second gas: chlorine (damp litmus paper bleached).
exercises.full_solution: Limewater turning milky is specifically the carbon dioxide test; damp litmus paper being bleached (turned white) is specifically the chlorine test, distinct from ammonia (which turns damp red litmus blue, rather than bleaching it).
common_errors: Confusing chlorine's bleaching effect with ammonia's colour-change effect on litmus paper, since both tests use litmus paper.

exercises.statement: A student reports: 'I added a reagent and a white precipitate formed, so the solution must contain chloride ions.' Explain what information is missing from this statement, and why it cannot be trusted as written.
hints: Recall which other ion also gives a white precipitate, with a different reagent.
Decide what single extra piece of information would make the statement trustworthy.
exercises.answer: The reagent used is missing. A white precipitate could indicate chloride (if the reagent was acidified silver nitrate) or sulfate (if the reagent was acidified barium nitrate) — without stating which reagent was actually added, the white precipitate alone cannot distinguish between these two completely different ions.
exercises.full_solution: Chloride and sulfate both give a white precipitate with their respective (different) reagents; reporting only the colour of the precipitate, without the reagent, leaves the result genuinely ambiguous between at least two different valid conclusions.
common_errors: Accepting the student's conclusion simply because chloride is often the first halide test learned, without checking whether the missing reagent information could point elsewhere.

exercises.statement: A water-quality inspector needs to check a river sample for contamination by a chloride-containing industrial waste, but the river water is also known to contain natural carbonate minerals. Using the reagent-observation-inference discipline from this lesson, explain the exact procedure the inspector should follow, and why skipping a step could give a misleading result about the contamination.
hints: Identify which ion (carbonate) could interfere with a direct chloride test here, exactly as in this lesson's main example.
State the full three-part chain for the final test, not just the final reagent.
exercises.answer: The inspector should first acidify the water sample with dilute nitric acid, to react away any natural carbonate present (releasing it as carbon dioxide gas), then add silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate at this stage is reliable evidence of chloride contamination. Skipping the acidification step could let the naturally occurring carbonate react with the silver nitrate directly, producing a precipitate even in a river sample with no industrial chloride contamination at all — a false positive that would wrongly suggest contamination.
exercises.full_solution: The inspector should first acidify the water sample with dilute nitric acid, to react away any natural carbonate present (releasing it as carbon dioxide gas), then add silver nitrate solution. A white precipitate at this stage is reliable evidence of chloride contamination. Skipping the acidification step could let the naturally occurring carbonate react with the silver nitrate directly, producing a precipitate even in a river sample with no industrial chloride contamination at all — a false positive that would wrongly suggest contamination.
common_errors: Suggesting the test can skip acidification because 'the river water is probably fine', without recognising that skipping the step specifically risks a false positive from the carbonate already known to be present.

exam_questions.statement: A solid is suspected to be a sulfate salt that might also contain carbonate as an impurity. (a) Describe the full test that would confirm sulfate while ruling out any interference from carbonate. (b) Explain, in terms of what carbonate would otherwise do, why the acidification step in your answer to (a) is necessary. (c) A separate sample of the same solid, when warmed with sodium hydroxide solution and a small piece of aluminium foil, releases a gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue. What does this show?
hints: Part (a) should name the specific acid used to acidify (and avoid any acid that already contains sulfate ions) as well as the barium reagent.
Part (c) should match the exact observation described to one specific ion test from this lesson.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate; a white precipitate confirms sulfate. (b) Without acidification, any carbonate impurity present would itself react with barium nitrate to form a precipitate, which could be mistaken for a sulfate-positive result even if no sulfate were actually present. (c) A gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue, released on warming with sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil, is ammonia, which confirms nitrate ions are present in the solid.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate; a white precipitate confirms sulfate. (b) Without acidification, any carbonate impurity present would itself react with barium nitrate to form a precipitate, which could be mistaken for a sulfate-positive result even if no sulfate were actually present. (c) A gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue, released on warming with sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil, is ammonia, which confirms nitrate ions are present in the solid.
mark_scheme: Correct acid (dilute nitric acid) and reagent (aqueous barium nitrate) named in part (a) (1 mark).
Correct observation (white precipitate) stated in part (a) (1 mark).
Explanation in part (b) correctly states that carbonate would otherwise also precipitate with the test reagent, risking a false positive (1 mark).
Nitrate correctly identified in part (c), with reference to the ammonia gas and litmus observation (1 mark).
common_errors: Acidifying with dilute sulfuric acid in part (a), which adds sulfate ions and makes the test give a white precipitate whether or not the sample contains sulfate.

exam_questions.statement: A gas produced in a reaction is tested with a glowing splint, which relights. (a) Identify the gas. (b) Explain, in terms of combustion, why this specific observation is evidence for this gas and not for hydrogen. (c) A student also claims a second, different gas sample 'relit a glowing splint with a loud pop'. Explain why this combined description cannot be correct for any single gas in this lesson's table.
hints: Part (b) should explain what a glowing splint relighting actually requires chemically.
Part (c) should check both halves of the claimed description against the gas-test table separately.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) A glowing splint relights only when extra oxygen is available to support its combustion; hydrogen does not support another substance's combustion in this way; instead hydrogen itself burns, producing a pop with a lighted (not glowing) splint, a completely different test. (c) 'Relighting a glowing splint' is the oxygen test and 'a loud pop' is the hydrogen test; no single gas in the table produces both effects together, so the student's combined description must be a mistaken mixing of the two separate tests.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Oxygen. (b) A glowing splint relights only when extra oxygen is available to support its combustion; hydrogen does not support another substance's combustion in this way; instead hydrogen itself burns, producing a pop with a lighted (not glowing) splint, a completely different test. (c) 'Relighting a glowing splint' is the oxygen test and 'a loud pop' is the hydrogen test; no single gas in the table produces both effects together, so the student's combined description must be a mistaken mixing of the two separate tests.
mark_scheme: Oxygen correctly identified in part (a) (1 mark).
Explanation in part (b) correctly distinguishes 'supports combustion' (oxygen) from 'itself burns' (hydrogen) (2 marks).
Explanation in part (c) correctly identifies that the two described effects belong to two different, separate gas tests (1 mark).
common_errors: In part (c), accepting the student's claim as a valid (if unusual) description of one gas, instead of recognising it mixes two separate tests.

challenge_questions.statement: An unknown solid gives the following results: Test 1, dilute acid added, no effervescence observed. Test 2, dissolved in water, acidified with dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate added: a cream precipitate forms. A classmate claims the solid 'must contain both carbonate and chloride'. Evaluate this claim using both test results, and state what the solid is most likely to contain instead.
hints: Check Test 1 against the carbonate test's expected positive result before accepting or rejecting it.
Check the precipitate colour in Test 2 carefully against the specific halide it matches.
challenge_questions.answer: The claim is incorrect on both counts. Test 1 shows no effervescence, which rules out carbonate (a carbonate would effervesce with dilute acid), so the solid does not contain carbonate. Test 2's cream precipitate (not white) is specifically the bromide test's result, not chloride's; so the solid most likely contains bromide ions, not chloride.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Test 1's negative result (no effervescence) is itself informative evidence against carbonate being present, just as a positive result would be evidence for it; a negative result should not simply be ignored. Test 2's precipitate colour must be matched precisely against the halide table: cream specifically indicates bromide, and mistaking it for chloride's white precipitate would lead to the wrong ion being identified entirely.
common_errors: Treating the negative result in Test 1 as uninformative and skipping straight to interpreting Test 2, instead of using both results together.
Assuming any precipitate from silver nitrate must be chloride, without checking its specific colour against the table.

mcq.stem: A solution forms a white precipitate when a reagent is added. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The solution must contain chloride ions, since white precipitates always indicate chloride.
options.why_wrong: sulfate also gives a white precipitate, but with a different reagent (acidified barium nitrate, not silver nitrate); colour alone cannot distinguish the two.

options.text: The solution must contain sulfate ions, since white precipitates always indicate sulfate.
options.why_wrong: chloride also gives a white precipitate, but with a different reagent (acidified silver nitrate); colour alone cannot distinguish the two.

options.text: The ion present cannot be determined from the colour alone; the specific reagent used must also be known.
No conclusion is possible from a precipitate test under any circumstances.
options.why_wrong: a precipitate test is genuinely useful evidence once the specific reagent used is also stated; the issue is only that colour alone, without the reagent, is ambiguous.

mcq.explanation: Both chloride (with acidified silver nitrate) and sulfate (with acidified barium nitrate) give a white precipitate; the reagent used must be stated alongside the colour for the result to identify a specific ion.

mcq.stem: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate solution when testing for a halide ion?

options.text: It is an optional step that makes the precipitate colour easier to see, but does not affect the result's validity.
options.why_wrong: the acidification step removes a specific source of interference (carbonate); omitting it risks a genuinely misleading, false-positive result, not just a cosmetic difference.

options.text: To dissolve the halide ion so that it can be detected at all.
options.why_wrong: the halide ion is already dissolved in solution before this test begins; acidification is not what makes it detectable, it is what rules out an interfering ion.

options.text: To directly produce the precipitate itself, before silver nitrate is even added.
options.why_wrong: the acid itself does not produce the halide precipitate; the precipitate forms afterwards, when silver nitrate reacts specifically with the halide ion.

options.text: To react away any carbonate ions present, which would otherwise also form a precipitate with silver nitrate and could be mistaken for a halide.

mcq.explanation: Carbonate ions would also form a precipitate with silver nitrate; acidifying first removes this carbonate as carbon dioxide gas, so a precipitate observed afterwards can only be explained by the halide ion being tested for.

mcq.stem: Which pair of observations is correctly matched to hydrogen and oxygen gas?

options.text: Hydrogen: a pop with a lighted splint. Oxygen: a glowing splint relights.
Hydrogen: a glowing splint relights. Oxygen: a pop with a lighted splint.
options.why_wrong: this swaps the two tests: a glowing splint relighting is oxygen's test (it supports the splint's combustion), while a pop with a lighted splint is hydrogen's test (the gas itself burns).

options.text: Both hydrogen and oxygen relight a glowing splint.
options.why_wrong: only oxygen relights a glowing splint; hydrogen is identified by a pop with a lighted splint, a different test using a different splint state.

options.text: Both hydrogen and oxygen produce a pop with a lighted splint.
options.why_wrong: only hydrogen produces a pop with a lighted splint; oxygen is identified by relighting a glowing splint instead.

mcq.explanation: Hydrogen itself burns rapidly, giving a pop with a lighted splint; oxygen supports combustion, so it relights a glowing splint — two different tests for two different reasons.

mcq.stem: A gas turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is this, and what does a second gas do differently that could be confused with it?

options.text: Chlorine turns damp red litmus blue; ammonia instead bleaches damp litmus paper white.
options.why_wrong: this swaps the two gases: chlorine is the one that bleaches litmus paper, while ammonia is the one that turns damp red litmus blue.

options.text: Ammonia turns damp red litmus blue; chlorine instead bleaches damp litmus paper white, a different effect.
Carbon dioxide turns damp red litmus blue.
options.why_wrong: carbon dioxide is identified by turning limewater milky, not by any litmus-paper colour change.

options.text: Both ammonia and chlorine turn damp red litmus paper blue.
options.why_wrong: only ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue; chlorine instead bleaches litmus paper, turning it white, which is a visually different result.

mcq.explanation: Ammonia (an alkaline gas) turns damp red litmus paper blue; chlorine instead bleaches litmus paper, turning it white — both use litmus paper, but with opposite-looking results.

flashcards.front: How do you tell apart a chloride and a sulfate result, since both give a white precipitate?
flashcards.back: By the reagent used: acidified silver nitrate giving a white precipitate indicates chloride; acidified barium nitrate giving a white precipitate indicates sulfate. The colour alone cannot distinguish them.

flashcards.front: Is acidifying before a halide or sulfate test an optional step?
flashcards.back: No. It removes interference from carbonate ions, which would otherwise also form a precipitate with the test reagent and risk a false positive.

flashcards.front: What are the tests for hydrogen and oxygen gas?
flashcards.back: Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen: a glowing splint relights.

flashcards.front: What are the tests for ammonia and chlorine gas using litmus paper?
flashcards.back: Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue. Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, turning it white.

flashcards.front: What three parts must a valid qualitative test report include?
flashcards.back: The reagent or action used, the observation that resulted, and the inference that observation supports — never the observation alone.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any white precipitate formed during a test is evidence for chloride ions.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Chloride's test (silver nitrate) is often the first precipitate test learned, so 'white precipitate' can become wrongly fixed in memory as meaning chloride specifically, regardless of which reagent produced it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner identifies chloride from a white precipitate without checking which reagent was used, even when the reagent was actually barium nitrate (testing for sulfate) or another precipitating agent entirely.
misconceptions.correct_model: A precipitate's colour is only meaningful once paired with the specific reagent that produced it: a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate indicates chloride, while a white precipitate with acidified barium nitrate indicates sulfate instead. The colour alone, without stating the reagent, is not enough evidence to identify an ion.
misconceptions.remediation: Always state the full chain: reagent used, then observation, then inference — never report just the observation and jump straight to a conclusion.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Acidifying the solution before adding the test reagent is an optional extra step that does not affect the result.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Acidification is often just one instruction in a longer list of steps, so its specific purpose can be overlooked if it is not explained.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner omits the acidification step when describing a halide or sulfate test, or cannot explain what would go wrong if it were skipped.
misconceptions.correct_model: Acidification (dilute nitric acid before silver nitrate for halides; dilute nitric acid before barium nitrate for sulfate) removes interference from other ions, particularly carbonate ions, which would otherwise also form a precipitate with these same reagents and could be mistaken for a positive halide or sulfate result. Skipping acidification risks a false positive, not simply a less careful procedure.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly: if carbonate ions were also present and acidification were skipped, would the test reagent still form a precipitate anyway? If yes, the acidification step is essential, not optional, to rule that out first.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Hydrogen gas relights a glowing splint, and oxygen gas makes a popping sound with a lit splint.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both tests involve a splint and both produce a dramatic, memorable effect, so the two gases' correct tests can be swapped in memory.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes hydrogen as relighting a glowing splint, or oxygen as producing a pop with a lit splint — the two tests reversed.
misconceptions.correct_model: Hydrogen gas gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint (the hydrogen itself burns rapidly); oxygen gas relights a glowing splint (the splint bursts back into flame because extra oxygen is available to support its combustion). The two tests use different splint states (lit versus glowing) precisely because they test for different things: whether the gas itself is flammable, or whether the gas supports something else's combustion.
misconceptions.remediation: Connect each test to what it is actually checking: a lit splint 'popping' tests whether the gas itself burns explosively (hydrogen); a glowing splint relighting tests whether the gas supports combustion of something else (oxygen).

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the colour of a precipitate and concluding an ion's identity without stating the reagent used.
common_mistakes.why: The colour is the most visually memorable part of the result, so the reagent that produced it can be left out of the final answer.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always write the full chain: reagent/acidification, then observation, then inference.

common_mistakes.mistake: Omitting the acidification step before a halide or sulfate test.
common_mistakes.why: Acidification can seem like a minor preparatory step rather than an essential part of the test.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Explain, each time, what carbonate interference the acidification step is specifically ruling out.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swapping the hydrogen (pop) and oxygen (relights) tests.
common_mistakes.why: Both tests use a splint and produce a dramatic effect, which can blur together in memory.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Link each test to what it actually checks: a pop means the gas itself is flammable (hydrogen); relighting means the gas supports combustion (oxygen).

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing ammonia's litmus colour change with chlorine's litmus bleaching.
common_mistakes.why: Both tests use damp litmus paper, so the two different effects can be mixed up.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember ammonia changes colour (red to blue); chlorine removes colour entirely (bleaches to white).

exam_notes: Always state the exact reagent (including which acid, for acidified tests) rather than a vague description like 'added a chemical'.
When two different ions can give the same observation (such as chloride and sulfate's white precipitates), name both possibilities and explain how the reagent used distinguishes them.
For gas tests, state the exact observation precisely (for example 'relights a glowing splint', not just 'reacts with a splint'), since examiners usually require the specific wording.
When a question gives a negative result (no effervescence, no precipitate), use it as evidence too, rather than only commenting on positive results.

summary.big_idea: A qualitative test is only valid evidence when the reagent (and any acidification), the observation and the inference are all stated together; the same observation (such as a white precipitate) can come from different reagents testing for completely different ions.
key_points: Carbonate, chloride, bromide, iodide, sulfate and nitrate each have a specific reagent, acidification requirement (where relevant), and resulting observation that must all be stated together.
Acidifying before a halide or sulfate test removes carbonate interference, preventing a false positive.
Chloride and sulfate both give a white precipitate; only the reagent used (silver nitrate versus barium nitrate) distinguishes them.
Hydrogen (pop with a lighted splint) and oxygen (relights a glowing splint) test for opposite properties: whether the gas itself burns, or whether it supports combustion.
Ammonia turns damp red litmus blue; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white — both use litmus paper but give opposite-looking results.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Never report just the observation: state the reagent, the observation and the inference together, every time.

06_Cations_precipitates_and_flame_tests..title: Cations, precipitates and flame tests
06_Cations_precipitates_and_flame_tests..subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Distinguish the cations ammonium, calcium, copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) and zinc using aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia, including what happens in excess of each reagent.
Identify lithium, sodium, potassium and copper(II) ions from the colour each produces in a flame test.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the reagent-observation-inference chain, and the principle that a single matching observation can be ambiguous, to identify an unknown (from an earlier lesson: test-observation-inference logic).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Cation identification in this lesson depends even more heavily on combining several observations together; without already expecting a single result to be ambiguous on its own, the need for a second reagent and excess behaviour will not make sense.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that an ionic compound is made of charged ions, named with a charge such as $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ (from C02: ions).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every test in this lesson is reported in terms of a specific named cation; without already being comfortable with ion names and charges, the table of results cannot be connected to an actual unknown sample.

theory_blocks.title: A pattern across reagents, not one colour
theory_blocks.body:
Several of this lesson's cations give a similarly coloured precipitate with sodium hydroxide at first glance, so no single observation can safely identify a cation on its own.

Reliable identification instead comes from a [[blue:**pattern**]]: the precipitate's colour with sodium hydroxide, what happens when sodium hydroxide is added in excess, and (where needed) the same two checks repeated with aqueous ammonia instead.

Only once this full pattern is assembled does the evidence point to one cation unambiguously.

theory_blocks.title: Cation tests with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia
theory_blocks.body:
| Cation | With NaOH (a few drops) | With excess NaOH | With $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$ (a few drops) | With excess $\mathrm{NH_{3}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ | White precipitate | Insoluble (stays white) | No precipitate, or only a very slight white precipitate | No further change |
| $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ | Light blue precipitate | Insoluble (stays light blue) | Light blue precipitate | Dissolves to a dark (deep) blue solution |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ | Green precipitate | Insoluble (stays green) | Green precipitate | Insoluble (stays green) |
| $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ | Red-brown precipitate | Insoluble (stays red-brown) | Red-brown precipitate | Insoluble (stays red-brown) |
| $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ | White precipitate | Dissolves to a colourless solution | White precipitate | Dissolves to a colourless solution |
| $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$ | No precipitate; ammonia gas released on warming (turns damp red litmus blue) | — | — | — |

Calcium and zinc share the same initial white precipitate with sodium hydroxide, but only zinc's dissolves in excess; copper(II)'s precipitate is unique in dissolving in excess ammonia but not in excess sodium hydroxide.

theory_blocks.title: A strategy for an unknown cation
theory_blocks.body:
1. Add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution. No precipitate at all, combined with the smell of ammonia on warming, identifies ammonium directly, with no further test needed.
2. If a precipitate forms, note its colour: green points to iron(II); red-brown points to iron(III); light blue points to copper(II); white points to either calcium or zinc (not yet distinguished).
3. Add more sodium hydroxide (excess). A white precipitate that dissolves to a colourless solution confirms zinc; a white precipitate that stays confirms calcium.
4. If ammonia is used instead of (or as well as) sodium hydroxide, a light blue precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia specifically (to a dark blue solution) confirms copper(II), distinguishing it from any other blue-ish precipitate.

Every cation in this table is reached by combining at least two separate observations; no single step on its own is sufficient for every case.

theory_blocks.title: A precipitate can still change after it forms
Flame tests
theory_blocks.body:
A flame test identifies certain metal ions directly from the colour they give a flame. A clean nichrome (or platinum) wire is dipped in dilute hydrochloric acid and rinsed,

then dipped into the solid or solution being tested, and held in a roaring (blue) Bunsen flame.

| Ion | Flame colour |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Li^+}$ | Red |
| $\mathrm{Na^+}$ | Yellow (orange-yellow) |
| $\mathrm{K^+}$ | Lilac |
| $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ | Blue-green |

A flame test is quick and needs only a tiny sample, but in this course it is used to identify only the four ions above (other metal ions, such as calcium, also colour a flame, but are not required here);

it gives no information about any anion present, and a mixture containing more than one of these ions can give a blended or masked colour, so it is most reliable on a sample suspected to contain only one of them.

assets.caption: A flame test: a nichrome wire loop carrying a small sample of the ion is held in a roaring Bunsen flame; the colour produced (shown as a reference key alongside) identifies lithium, sodium, potassium or copper(II) directly.
assets.purpose: Show the flame-test apparatus and give a visual reference key for the four required flame colours alongside it.

theory_blocks.title: Completing the qualitative analysis picture
theory_blocks.body:
Across this unit, every identification technique has followed the same underlying discipline: a reagent or action, a precise observation, and an inference that only follows once enough evidence has been combined.

Anions (the previous lesson) are identified from acidification plus a precipitate or gas; cations (this lesson) are identified from a pattern across two reagents, their excess behaviour, and sometimes a flame colour.

A full, unknown ionic compound is identified by combining one anion test with one cation test, never by either alone.

keywords.definition: Adding more of a reagent than needed for the first visible reaction, used to test whether a precipitate dissolves further.
A test that identifies certain metal ions from the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen flame.
An insoluble solid that forms and separates out when a reagent is added to a solution.

worked_examples.statement: **A precipitate colour that identifies a cation directly.** A solution forms a red-brown precipitate on adding sodium hydroxide, which stays red-brown even in excess sodium hydroxide. Identify the cation.
knowns: Precipitate colour: red-brown
Insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide
reasoning: Red-brown is the distinctive colour given only by iron(III) among this lesson's cations.
Iron(III)'s precipitate is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide, which matches the given result and rules out any cation that dissolves in excess.
worked_examples.solution: The cation is iron(III), $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Red-brown is unique enough among this lesson's cations to identify iron(III) from the colour alone, though confirming it stays insoluble in excess adds further confidence.

worked_examples.statement: **Distinguishing calcium from zinc.** Two unlabelled solutions, P and Q, each form a white precipitate on adding a few drops of sodium hydroxide. On adding excess sodium hydroxide, P's precipitate dissolves to a colourless solution, while Q's precipitate remains white and undissolved. Identify the cation in each solution.
knowns: Both P and Q: white precipitate with a few drops of NaOH
P: precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH
Q: precipitate stays white in excess NaOH
unknowns: Identity of the cation in P and in Q
reasoning: Both calcium and zinc give an initial white precipitate, so the first observation alone cannot distinguish P from Q.
Only zinc's white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, to a colourless solution: this matches solution P exactly.
Only calcium's white precipitate stays insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide: this matches solution Q exactly.
worked_examples.solution: Solution P contains zinc, $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ (precipitate dissolves in excess). Solution Q contains calcium, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ (precipitate stays insoluble in excess).
worked_examples.interpretation: The two solutions were genuinely indistinguishable after the first observation alone; only the excess-reagent step provided the evidence needed to tell them apart.

worked_examples.statement: **Confirming copper(II) specifically.** A solution gives a light blue precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide. A student assumes this alone confirms copper(II). Explain why a further test is needed, and describe the test that would confirm it.
knowns: Light blue precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide
unknowns: Why a further test is needed, and what that test is
reasoning: Among this lesson's cations, light blue is distinctive enough that no other listed cation shares it with sodium hydroxide alone, but relying on colour alone still repeats the same risky habit this unit has been warning against throughout.

A fully convincing confirmation instead checks the excess behaviour with a second reagent: copper(II)'s precipitate is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide but dissolves in excess ammonia, to a dark blue solution — a very specific, unique pattern.
Testing with aqueous ammonia (a few drops, then excess) and observing this exact pattern removes any remaining doubt, rather than relying on a colour judgement by eye alone.
worked_examples.solution:
A further test is needed because relying on a single colour observation, even a fairly distinctive one, does not follow the full reagent-pattern discipline used throughout this unit.

Testing with aqueous ammonia and observing the precipitate dissolve in excess to a dark blue solution confirms copper(II) specifically.
worked_examples.interpretation: Even when a first observation looks fairly conclusive, the stronger habit is to complete the full pattern (second reagent, excess behaviour) before finalising an identification.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Accepting a single, seemingly distinctive colour as sufficient evidence, instead of applying the same full-pattern discipline used for every other cation in this lesson.

worked_examples.statement: **A full two-stage cation identification.** An unknown solid is dissolved in water. Test 1: a few drops of sodium hydroxide give a white precipitate; excess sodium hydroxide dissolves it to a colourless solution. Test 2: a flame test on a separate sample gives no useful colour (the solid contains no lithium, sodium, potassium or copper). (a) Identify the cation from Test 1 alone, with reasoning. (b) Explain what Test 2 does, and does not, rule out. (c) Suggest one anion test (from the previous lesson) that would usefully complete the identification of the whole compound.
knowns: Test 1: white precipitate with NaOH, dissolves in excess
Test 2: flame test gives no useful colour
unknowns: Cation identity, scope of Test 2, and a suggested anion test
reasoning: (a) A white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide is specifically zinc's pattern among this lesson's cations, so the cation is zinc.

(b) Zinc is not one of the four ions a flame test identifies (lithium, sodium, potassium, copper), so a flame test giving no useful colour is entirely consistent with zinc;

it does not contradict the Test 1 result, it simply does not add any new cation evidence here.

(c) Any of the previous lesson's anion tests (for example, acidified silver nitrate for a halide, or acidified barium nitrate for sulfate) would identify the anion, completing the full compound's identity alongside the cation evidence from Test 1.
worked_examples.interpretation: A 'negative' flame-test result still needs to be interpreted correctly: it only means none of the four flame-test ions are present, not that no cation at all is present.

guided_exercises.statement: A solution gives a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide, which remains green and insoluble even in excess sodium hydroxide. Identify the cation, and state one further check that could rule out it being mistaken for iron(III) on a later inspection.
hints: Match the precipitate colour directly against the cation table.
Recall the caveat about one of the iron precipitates slowly changing appearance on standing.
guided_exercises.answer: Iron(II), $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$. A later check should note that a green precipitate can develop a brown tinge at its surface on standing, so the colour should ideally be read as the precipitate first forms, not after it has been left for some time, to avoid confusing it with a fresh iron(III) result.
common_errors: Assuming any brownish tinge seen later must mean the sample is actually iron(III), without considering that iron(II)'s own precipitate can change appearance on standing.

guided_exercises.statement: A flame test gives a lilac flame colour. A second, separate flame test on a different sample gives a blue-green flame colour. Identify the ion in each case.
hints: Match each described colour directly against the flame-colour table.
Check that neither colour is being confused with a similar-sounding one (for example lilac versus red).
guided_exercises.answer: Lilac flame: potassium, $\mathrm{K^+}$. Blue-green flame: copper(II), $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$.
common_errors: Confusing lilac (potassium) with red (lithium), since both are described loosely as 'purple-ish' shades by some learners.

exercises.statement: Two solutions each form a precipitate with sodium hydroxide: solution R forms a green precipitate, solution S forms a red-brown precipitate. State the cation in each, and explain why 'both are iron, so both look the same' is incorrect.
hints: Match each described colour directly against the table.
State explicitly what charge each iron ion carries.
exercises.answer: Solution R: iron(II), $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ (green precipitate). Solution S: iron(III), $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ (red-brown precipitate). 'Both are iron, so both look the same' is incorrect because iron(II) and iron(III) are different ions, with different charges (2+ and 3+), and give clearly different, distinguishable precipitate colours, despite both containing the same element.
exercises.full_solution: The precipitate colour depends on the specific ion present, not merely on which element it contains; iron(II) and iron(III) are chemically distinct ions and are correctly distinguished by colour (green versus red-brown), exactly as any two unrelated cations would be.
common_errors: Assuming both iron ions must give the same result simply because they share the element name 'iron'.

exercises.statement: A solution gives no precipitate at all when sodium hydroxide is added. When the mixture is then warmed, a gas is released that turns damp red litmus paper blue. Identify the cation present.
hints: Recall which cation in this lesson's table gives no precipitate with sodium hydroxide under any condition.
Match the gas description to a specific gas test from the previous lesson.
exercises.answer: Ammonium, $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$. No precipitate at all with sodium hydroxide, combined with ammonia gas released on warming (confirmed by the damp red litmus paper turning blue), is ammonium's distinctive pattern.
exercises.full_solution: Ammonium is the only cation in this lesson's table that gives no precipitate with sodium hydroxide under any circumstance; instead, warming releases ammonia gas directly from the ammonium ion reacting with the hydroxide, identified by the standard ammonia gas test (damp red litmus turning blue) from the previous lesson.
common_errors: Concluding 'no cation is present' simply because no precipitate formed, instead of recognising that ammonium's own test specifically does not involve a precipitate at all.

exercises.statement: A solution gives a white precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide. A student wants to identify the cation but only has sodium hydroxide available, not ammonia. Using excess sodium hydroxide alone, state what single further observation would let the student decide between the two possible candidates, and what each outcome would mean.
hints: Recall which two cations both give an initial white precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
Decide what the single further step (excess sodium hydroxide) would need to show to distinguish them, without needing ammonia at all.
exercises.answer: Adding excess sodium hydroxide and observing whether the precipitate dissolves is sufficient: if the white precipitate dissolves to a colourless solution, the cation is zinc; if it remains white and undissolved, the cation is calcium. Ammonia is not needed to distinguish these two specifically, since excess sodium hydroxide alone already tells them apart.
exercises.full_solution: Calcium and zinc are the two cations sharing an initial white precipitate with sodium hydroxide; their excess-sodium-hydroxide behaviour (zinc dissolves, calcium does not) is already sufficient to distinguish them without needing a second reagent at all, unlike copper(II), which specifically needs ammonia to be fully confirmed.
common_errors: Assuming ammonia is always required to distinguish any two cations sharing an initial colour, when calcium and zinc can in fact already be told apart using sodium hydroxide alone.

exercises.statement: A quality-control chemist is validating a new, unfamiliar reagent that is claimed to form a precipitate with a certain metal ion. A colleague says 'once we've seen the precipitate form, there's no need to test what happens with more of the reagent — the identification is already complete.' Using the excess-reagent principle from this lesson, evaluate this claim and suggest what the chemist should actually do.
hints: Recall which two cations in this lesson's table would have been wrongly treated as 'already identified' if only the first precipitate had been checked.
State the general principle this transfers, not just the specific calcium/zinc example.
exercises.answer: The colleague's claim is incorrect. As with calcium and zinc in this lesson, two different ions can give an identical-looking first precipitate with any given reagent, and only the behaviour in excess reveals whether they are actually different. The chemist should always test the reagent in excess as a required second step, not an optional extra, before treating any new reagent's result as a complete identification.
exercises.full_solution: The colleague's claim is incorrect. As with calcium and zinc in this lesson, two different ions can give an identical-looking first precipitate with any given reagent, and only the behaviour in excess reveals whether they are actually different. The chemist should always test the reagent in excess as a required second step, not an optional extra, before treating any new reagent's result as a complete identification.
common_errors: Treating the excess-reagent check as something specific to sodium hydroxide and ammonia only, rather than recognising it as a general principle that applies to validating any new reagent.

exam_questions.statement: A solution gives a light blue precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide. (a) State one cation this observation is consistent with. (b) Describe the two further tests (one with excess sodium hydroxide, one with aqueous ammonia) that would fully confirm this cation's identity, and state the expected result of each. (c) Explain why checking only the first observation would not meet the standard of evidence used throughout this unit.
hints: Part (b) should give the expected result in excess of each named reagent separately.
Part (c) should refer to the general reagent-observation-inference discipline, not just this one cation.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Copper(II), $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$. (b) In excess sodium hydroxide, the light blue precipitate should remain insoluble (stays light blue). In excess aqueous ammonia, the light blue precipitate should dissolve to a dark (deep) blue solution. Observing both confirms copper(II) specifically. (c) This unit has consistently treated a single observation as insufficient, ambiguous evidence; completing the excess-reagent pattern with both reagents is what turns 'consistent with copper(II)' into a confirmed identification.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Copper(II), $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$. (b) In excess sodium hydroxide, the light blue precipitate should remain insoluble (stays light blue). In excess aqueous ammonia, the light blue precipitate should dissolve to a dark (deep) blue solution. Observing both confirms copper(II) specifically. (c) This unit has consistently treated a single observation as insufficient, ambiguous evidence; completing the excess-reagent pattern with both reagents is what turns 'consistent with copper(II)' into a confirmed identification.
mark_scheme: Copper(II) correctly named in part (a) (1 mark).
Correct excess-NaOH result (remains insoluble) stated in part (b) (1 mark).
Correct excess-NH3 result (dissolves to dark blue solution) stated in part (b) (1 mark).
Explanation in part (c) correctly refers to the single-observation-is-ambiguous principle used throughout the unit (1 mark).
common_errors: Giving the excess-ammonia result correctly but stating the precipitate also dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, when copper(II)'s precipitate specifically does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

exam_questions.statement: A solid compound is analysed. Flame test: the flame turns a clear lilac colour. Sodium hydroxide test on a separate dissolved sample: no precipitate forms, and warming the mixture releases a gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue. (a) What does the flame test show, and what does it rule out? (b) What does the sodium hydroxide and warming test show? (c) Explain whether these two results are consistent with each other, or contradictory, and why.
hints: Part (a) should name the ion the flame colour identifies, and state which other flame-test ions are ruled out by a single clear colour.
Part (c) should consider whether a compound can contain more than one kind of positively charged particle at once.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The lilac flame identifies potassium, $\mathrm{K^+}$, and rules out lithium, sodium and copper(II) (none of which give lilac). (b) No precipitate with sodium hydroxide, plus ammonia gas released on warming, is ammonium's distinctive pattern, confirming ammonium, $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$, is also present. (c) The two results are not contradictory: a single compound can contain more than one type of cation (here, both potassium and ammonium ions), so both results can be true for the same solid at once, as in a double salt.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The lilac flame identifies potassium, $\mathrm{K^+}$, and rules out lithium, sodium and copper(II) (none of which give lilac). (b) No precipitate with sodium hydroxide, plus ammonia gas released on warming, is ammonium's distinctive pattern, confirming ammonium, $\mathrm{NH_{4}^+}$, is also present. (c) The two results are not contradictory: a single compound can contain more than one type of cation (here, both potassium and ammonium ions), so both results can be true for the same solid at once, as in a double salt.
mark_scheme: Potassium correctly identified from the flame colour in part (a), with other flame ions correctly ruled out (1 mark).
Ammonium correctly identified from the sodium hydroxide/warming test in part (b) (1 mark).
Part (c) correctly states the two results are not contradictory (1 mark).
Part (c) correctly explains that a single compound can contain more than one cation (1 mark).
common_errors: Concluding in part (c) that the two results must be contradictory, since only one cation 'should' be present, without considering a compound containing two different cations.

challenge_questions.statement: An unknown solid gives the following results. Test 1 (NaOH, a few drops): white precipitate. Test 2 (excess NaOH): precipitate remains white and undissolved. Test 3 (flame test): none of the four reference flame colours (lithium red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, copper(II) blue-green) is seen. A classmate claims 'Test 3 is pointless here, since Tests 1 and 2 already identify the cation completely.' Evaluate this claim, stating the cation identified and what, if anything, Test 3 adds.
hints: Decide first whether Tests 1 and 2 alone are already sufficient to identify one specific cation from the table.
Consider what a negative flame-test result (none of the four reference colours) does, and does not, add once a cation has already been identified by a different method.
challenge_questions.answer: The cation is calcium, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$: Tests 1 and 2 together (white precipitate, insoluble in excess) already match calcium's pattern uniquely among this lesson's cations, so the identification is complete without Test 3. The classmate's claim is essentially correct for identifying the cation: calcium is not one of the four ions this course identifies by flame test, so Test 3 cannot confirm calcium. Its result is simply consistent with Tests 1-2, and the only extra information it adds is that lithium, sodium, potassium and copper(II) ions are not also present; it was not pointless to perform in general, but here the cation was already identified before Test 3 was carried out.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Calcium and zinc are the two cations that could initially be confused from Test 1 alone, but Test 2 (excess NaOH, precipitate remains white) is exactly calcium's distinctive result, uniquely distinguishing it from zinc without needing any further test. Since calcium is not among the four flame-test ions used in this course, a result showing none of those four colours neither confirms nor contradicts this; it only rules out lithium, sodium, potassium and copper(II) being present as well, which is a more precise and defensible answer than either 'pointless' or 'essential'.
common_errors: Concluding the cation cannot be identified at all because the flame test gave no useful result, without first checking whether Tests 1 and 2 had already uniquely identified it.
