Dismissing Test 3 as always pointless in general, rather than explaining specifically why it adds nothing in this particular case.

mcq.stem: A solution gives a white precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide. Which further observation would confirm the cation is calcium rather than zinc?

options.text: The precipitate is white.
options.why_wrong: both calcium and zinc give a white precipitate with a few drops of sodium hydroxide; the colour alone cannot distinguish them.

options.text: The precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to a colourless solution.
options.why_wrong: this is zinc's result, not calcium's; calcium's precipitate stays insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide.

options.text: The precipitate remains white and undissolved when excess sodium hydroxide is added.
A flame test gives a lilac colour.
options.why_wrong: calcium is not one of the four ions identified by a flame test in this lesson (lithium, sodium, potassium, copper(II)), and lilac specifically identifies potassium, not calcium.

mcq.explanation: Calcium's white precipitate stays insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide, while zinc's dissolves to a colourless solution; this excess behaviour is what distinguishes the two cations.

mcq.stem: Which statement about adding excess reagent to a cation precipitate is correct?

options.text: Adding excess reagent never changes a precipitate once it has formed.
options.why_wrong: zinc's precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide or excess ammonia, and copper(II)'s dissolves in excess ammonia specifically; excess reagent can and does change some precipitates.

options.text: Excess reagent only matters for anion tests, not cation tests.
options.why_wrong: excess-reagent behaviour is specifically how several cations in this lesson (zinc and copper(II)) are distinguished from similar-looking cations; it is central to this lesson's cation tests.

options.text: Every precipitate in this lesson's table dissolves if enough excess reagent is added.
options.why_wrong: calcium, iron(II) and iron(III) all remain insoluble even in excess of either reagent; not every precipitate dissolves in excess.

options.text: Some precipitates (such as zinc's or copper(II)'s under the right reagent) genuinely dissolve in excess, and this is important diagnostic evidence.

mcq.explanation: Excess-reagent behaviour genuinely distinguishes several cations (zinc dissolving, calcium not dissolving, in excess sodium hydroxide; copper(II) dissolving only in excess ammonia), so it is essential diagnostic evidence, not an irrelevant extra step.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes iron(II) and iron(III) with sodium hydroxide?

options.text: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate; iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate; both are insoluble in excess.
Both iron(II) and iron(III) give the same green precipitate, since both are iron.
options.why_wrong: iron(II) and iron(III) are different ions with different charges and give clearly different precipitate colours (green versus red-brown), despite sharing the same element.

options.text: Iron(II) gives a red-brown precipitate; iron(III) gives a green precipitate.
options.why_wrong: this swaps the two colours: iron(II) gives green, and iron(III) gives red-brown, not the other way round.

options.text: Iron(II) and iron(III) can only be told apart using a flame test.
options.why_wrong: neither iron(II) nor iron(III) is one of the four ions a flame test identifies in this lesson; they are distinguished by their different sodium hydroxide precipitate colours instead.

mcq.explanation: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate and iron(III) gives a red-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide; both stay insoluble in excess, and the clear colour difference distinguishes the two ions directly.

mcq.stem: A flame test gives a yellow flame colour. Which ion is present, and which ion would instead give a lilac colour?

options.text: Yellow: potassium. Lilac: sodium.
options.why_wrong: this swaps the two colours: sodium gives yellow, and potassium gives lilac, not the other way round.

options.text: Yellow: sodium. Lilac: potassium.
Yellow: lithium. Lilac: copper(II).
options.why_wrong: lithium gives a red flame, not yellow, and copper(II) gives a blue-green flame, not lilac.

options.text: Yellow: copper(II). Lilac: lithium.
options.why_wrong: copper(II) gives a blue-green flame, not yellow, and lithium gives a red flame, not lilac.

mcq.explanation: Sodium gives a yellow flame; potassium gives a lilac flame — these are two of the four flame colours required in this lesson, and are not interchangeable with lithium (red) or copper(II) (blue-green).

flashcards.front: How do you distinguish calcium and zinc, which both give a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide?
flashcards.back: By their behaviour in excess sodium hydroxide: zinc's precipitate dissolves to a colourless solution; calcium's stays insoluble (white).

flashcards.front: Does adding excess reagent to a precipitate ever matter?
flashcards.back: Yes. Zinc's precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH or excess NH3; copper(II)'s dissolves in excess NH3 specifically (not NaOH). Excess behaviour is essential diagnostic evidence.

flashcards.front: What colour precipitate does iron(II) give with sodium hydroxide, and what does iron(III) give?
flashcards.back: Iron(II): green. Iron(III): red-brown. Both stay insoluble in excess of either reagent.

flashcards.front: What are the four flame-test colours required in this lesson?
flashcards.back: Lithium: red. Sodium: yellow. Potassium: lilac. Copper(II): blue-green.

flashcards.front: A solution gives no precipitate with sodium hydroxide, but releases a gas on warming that turns damp red litmus blue. Which cation is this?
flashcards.back: Ammonium, NH4+ — no precipitate forms with sodium hydroxide; instead, warming releases ammonia gas directly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any white precipitate formed on adding sodium hydroxide solution identifies calcium ions.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Calcium's test is often the first cation precipitate test learned, so 'white precipitate with sodium hydroxide' can become fixed in memory as meaning calcium specifically.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner identifies calcium from a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide without checking what happens when excess sodium hydroxide is added.
misconceptions.correct_model: Both calcium and zinc ions give a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution; they are distinguished only by what happens in **excess**: calcium's white precipitate stays insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide, while zinc's white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to give a colourless solution. The initial colour alone cannot tell them apart.
misconceptions.remediation: After observing any white precipitate with sodium hydroxide, always add more (excess) sodium hydroxide and observe whether the precipitate dissolves or remains, before drawing a conclusion.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Once a precipitate has formed, adding more of the same reagent (excess) never changes anything further.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A precipitate looks like a finished, stable result, so continuing to add reagent after it forms can seem pointless.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner stops observing as soon as a precipitate forms, without testing what happens in excess reagent, even though the lesson's cations are specifically distinguished by their excess behaviour.
misconceptions.correct_model: Some precipitates genuinely dissolve when excess reagent is added: zinc's white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide or excess ammonia; copper(II)'s light blue precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia (to a dark blue solution) but not in excess sodium hydroxide. Excess-reagent behaviour is itself essential diagnostic evidence, not an irrelevant extra step.
misconceptions.remediation: Treat 'what happens in excess?' as a required second observation for every precipitate test in this lesson, not an optional check.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Iron(II) and iron(III) ions give the same coloured precipitate with sodium hydroxide, since both are 'iron'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both ions share the same element name (iron) and the same general reagent (sodium hydroxide), so it is easy to assume they must look the same.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports the same precipitate colour for both iron(II) and iron(III), or cannot state a colour difference between them.
misconceptions.correct_model: Iron(II) gives a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide, while iron(III) gives a distinctly different red-brown precipitate; both precipitates are insoluble in excess of either sodium hydroxide or ammonia. The two ions, despite sharing an element, are chemically different species with clearly different observable results.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the two precipitate colours directly, side by side, and connect the colour difference to the different charge (2+ versus 3+) on the same element's ion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Identifying calcium from a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide without checking excess.
common_mistakes.why: Calcium's test is often the first cation precipitate test learned, so 'white = calcium' can become fixed in memory.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always add excess sodium hydroxide and check whether the white precipitate dissolves (zinc) or remains (calcium) before concluding.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping observation as soon as a precipitate forms, without testing its behaviour in excess reagent.
common_mistakes.why: A precipitate looks like a finished, stable result.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Treat 'what happens in excess?' as a required step for every cation precipitate test in this lesson.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming iron(II) and iron(III) give the same result because they share the element name.
common_mistakes.why: The shared element name makes the two ions feel like they should behave identically.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Compare the two precipitate colours directly: green (iron(II)) versus red-brown (iron(III)).

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a negative flame-test result as meaning 'no cation is present'.
common_mistakes.why: A flame test can feel like a general-purpose cation test rather than one limited to four specific ions.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember a flame test only identifies lithium, sodium, potassium and copper(II); a negative result only rules out those four, nothing else.

exam_notes: Always state the result in both a few drops and in excess of the reagent, since examiners often award separate marks for each.
Name the specific reagent (sodium hydroxide or ammonia) alongside every precipitate observation, exactly as for the anion tests in the previous lesson.
When two cations share an initial observation, name both possibilities first, then state the further test that distinguishes them, rather than guessing one directly.
For flame tests, give the precise colour word used in the syllabus (for example 'lilac', not 'purple') since examiners mark against specific expected wording.

summary.big_idea: A cation is identified from a pattern across two reagents and their excess behaviour, not from one precipitate colour alone; four specific ions (lithium, sodium, potassium, copper(II)) can additionally be identified directly from a flame colour.
key_points: Calcium and zinc both give an initial white precipitate with sodium hydroxide; only their behaviour in excess (insoluble versus dissolves) tells them apart.
Copper(II) is confirmed by its precipitate dissolving in excess ammonia (to a dark blue solution) but not in excess sodium hydroxide.
Iron(II) (green) and iron(III) (red-brown) give clearly different precipitate colours, both insoluble in excess of either reagent.
Ammonium gives no precipitate with sodium hydroxide at all; it is identified instead by ammonia gas released on warming.
Flame tests identify lithium (red), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac) and copper(II) (blue-green) directly, but no other ion in this lesson.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Never stop at the first precipitate: check what happens in excess, and treat 'no change in excess' as real evidence too.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from experimental methods and analysis accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: What measuring device would you use to obtain values for: (a) the volume of liquid in a coffee mug; (b) the mass of an apple; (c) the temperature of a cup of tea; (d) the time taken to run up 20 stairs; (e) the time taken by an apple to fall through one metre?
exercises.answer: (a) A measuring cylinder (pour the liquid out of the mug into it). (b) An electronic (digital) balance. (c) A thermometer (liquid-in-glass or digital probe thermometer). (d) A stopwatch. (e) An electronic timer triggered by light gates (sensors), not a hand-operated stopwatch.
exercises.full_solution:
- **(a)** A measuring cylinder - pour the liquid out of the mug into it and read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
- **(b)** An electronic balance - the mass is read straight off the display.
- **(c)** A thermometer - with the bulb fully immersed in the tea and the eye level with the liquid column.
- **(d)** A stopwatch - the run lasts a few seconds, so the 0.2-0.3 s reaction time of the person pressing the button is only a small fraction of the reading.
- **(e)** An electronic timer triggered by light gates - not a hand-held stopwatch.

Why: the apple falls 1 m in only about 0.45 s (from $s=\frac{1}{2}gt^2$, $t=\sqrt{2\times 1/9.8}=0.45$ s), so a human reaction time of 0.2-0.3 s would be a large fraction of the time being measured. An automatic trigger removes that error. In every part, choose the instrument whose precision is good enough for the size of the quantity being measured.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Complete the table below by stating the typical accuracy of each of the measuring devices listed: stopwatch; digital timer; digital balance; liquid-in-glass thermometer; 100 ml measuring cylinder.
exercises.answer: stopwatch: to about 0.01 s on the display (but real timing by hand is limited by human reaction time, around ±0.2-0.3 s); digital timer (e.g. one triggered electronically, such as by a light gate): to about 0.01 s, and this full precision is actually achievable because no human reaction time is involved; digital balance: ±0.01 g; liquid-in-glass thermometer: ±0.5 °C for one graduated in 1 °C divisions (the chapter's '0.1 °C' claim applies only to a thermometer with much finer 0.1 °C graduations, which is unusual in a school lab); 100 ml measuring cylinder: ±0.5-1 cm³ (half of the smallest scale division, typically 1-2 cm³).
exercises.full_solution:
- Stopwatch: the display reads to 0.01 s, but started and stopped by hand it is only good to about ±0.2-0.3 s.
- Digital timer (triggered electronically, e.g. by a light gate): ±0.01 s.
- Digital balance: ±0.01 g.
- Liquid-in-glass thermometer graduated in 1 °C steps: ±0.5 °C.
- 100 cm³ measuring cylinder graduated every 1-2 cm³: ±0.5-1 cm³.

Why: an analogue scale can be read to about half its smallest division, and a digital display to its last digit - unless a human reaction time is added on top, which is exactly what limits the hand-held stopwatch. A measuring cylinder is therefore far less precise than a burette or a pipette.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Describe how you would use chromatography to show whether blue ink contains a single pure dye or a mixture of dyes.
exercises.answer: Put a small spot of the blue ink near the bottom of a piece of chromatography paper (above the level the solvent will reach), dip the bottom edge in a suitable solvent inside a covered beaker (without the solvent touching the spot), and let the solvent rise up the paper. Remove the paper once the solvent front has nearly reached the top and mark the solvent front, then let it dry. If only one spot (of one colour) appears on the finished chromatogram, the ink is a single pure dye; if two or more separate spots of different colours (or different Rf values) appear, the ink is a mixture of dyes.
exercises.full_solution:
- Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of a piece of chromatography paper and put a small, concentrated spot of the blue ink on it.
- Stand the paper in a shallow layer of a suitable solvent in a covered container, with the baseline above the solvent level so the spot does not dissolve into the pool.
- Let the solvent rise until the solvent front is near the top of the paper, then remove the paper, mark the solvent front at once and let it dry.
- **One spot = a single pure dye. Two or more spots = a mixture of dyes**, and each spot has its own $R_f$ value, where $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the spot}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$.

Why: different dyes have different solubilities in the solvent and are held by the paper to different extents, so they are carried up at different rates and separate out.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: What criteria can be used to test the purity of a substance?
exercises.answer: Melting point (a pure solid melts sharply at one fixed temperature; an impure solid melts gradually over a range of temperatures), boiling point (a pure liquid boils at one steady, fixed temperature; an impure liquid/solution boils over a range of temperatures), chromatography (a pure substance gives only one spot on a chromatogram; a mixture gives more than one spot), and solubility (a pure substance dissolves completely in a suitable solvent at a given temperature; any solid that remains undissolved indicates an insoluble impurity, which can be filtered off and identified).
exercises.full_solution:
- **Melting point** - a pure solid melts sharply at one fixed temperature; an impure solid melts lower and over a range.
- **Boiling point** - a pure liquid boils at one steady temperature; an impure liquid boils over a range.
- **Chromatography** - a pure substance gives one spot on the chromatogram; a mixture gives more than one.
- **Solubility** - a pure substance dissolves completely in a suitable solvent; any residue left undissolved is an insoluble impurity.

Why: an impurity disturbs the regular arrangement of particles in a solid and changes the composition of a liquid, so a fixed melting or boiling point becomes a range.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: What is the difference between simple distillation and fractional distillation?
exercises.answer: Simple distillation uses just a flask and a condenser and is used to separate a solvent from a solution (e.g. to get pure water out of salt water), or to separate liquids whose boiling points are very far apart; it cannot cleanly separate two miscible liquids that both evaporate and have fairly close boiling points. Fractional distillation adds a fractionating column (packed with glass beads/rods to give a large surface area) between the flask and the condenser, which lets vapour condense and re-evaporate repeatedly as it rises; this allows a mixture of two or more miscible liquids with close boiling points (e.g. ethanol, b.pt. 78 °C, and water, b.pt. 100 °C) to be separated out one component at a time, with the thermometer reading showing when each fraction has finished distilling over.
exercises.full_solution:
- **Simple distillation** uses only a flask and a condenser. It separates a solvent from a solution (such as pure water from salt water, because the salt does not evaporate) or liquids whose boiling points are very far apart.
- **Fractional distillation** adds a fractionating column, packed with glass beads or rods, between the flask and the condenser. It separates two or more miscible liquids with boiling points fairly close together, such as ethanol (b.pt. 78 °C) and water (b.pt. 100 °C).

Why: inside the column the rising vapour condenses and re-evaporates over and over on the large surface area, and each time the vapour that travels further up is richer in the lower-boiling liquid. The components therefore come over one at a time: the thermometer holds steady near 78 °C while the ethanol distils, then rises towards 100 °C when the water follows. Simple distillation has no column, so it cannot do this.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Devise a method for obtaining salt (sodium chloride) from sea water in the school laboratory.
exercises.answer: Filter the sea water first to remove any sand or other insoluble material. Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat it gently (e.g. over a water bath or a low Bunsen flame) to evaporate the water. The solubility of sodium chloride hardly changes with temperature, so cooling a hot saturated solution gives very few extra crystals: keep evaporating until most of the water has gone and plenty of salt crystals have formed, stopping just before the basin is completely dry to avoid spitting. Leave it to cool, filter off the salt crystals, rinse them with a very small amount of cold distilled water, and dry them between sheets of filter paper or in a warm (not too hot) oven. (The salt obtained still contains small amounts of the other salts dissolved in sea water.)
exercises.full_solution:
- Filter the sea water to remove sand and any other insoluble material; the salt stays dissolved in the filtrate.
- Heat the filtrate gently in an evaporating basin, ideally over a water bath, to evaporate the water.
- Stop once most of the water has gone and plenty of crystals have formed - just before the basin is dry, so the contents do not spit - and leave it to cool.
- Filter off the crystals, rinse them with a very little cold distilled water, and dry them between sheets of filter paper or in a warm oven.

Why: the solubility of sodium chloride hardly changes with temperature (about 36 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C and about 39 g at 100 °C), so cooling a hot saturated solution yields almost no extra crystals. The salt has to be obtained by evaporating the water away instead. Sea water also contains small amounts of other dissolved salts, so the product is not perfectly pure.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Which method would you use to separate: (a) coffee grains from coffee solution; (b) petrol (b.pt. 30 °C) from a crude oil; (c) pieces of steel from engine oil; (d) oxygen (b.pt. -183 °C) from liquid air?
exercises.answer: (a) Filtration. (b) Fractional distillation. (c) Filtration (steel is an insoluble solid in a liquid); since steel is magnetic, a magnet could also be used to lift the pieces out directly. (d) Fractional distillation of liquid air.
exercises.full_solution:
- **(a)** Filtration - the grains are an insoluble solid, so they stay on the filter paper as the residue while the solution runs through as the filtrate.
- **(b)** Fractional distillation - crude oil is a mixture of miscible liquids with a wide range of boiling points, and petrol (b.pt. about 30 °C) is one of the most volatile, so it distils over first.
- **(c)** Filtration - the steel pieces are an insoluble solid in a liquid. A magnet also works here, because steel is magnetic and the oil is not.
- **(d)** Fractional distillation - liquid air is a mixture of miscible liquids, and nitrogen (b.pt. -196 °C) boils off before oxygen (b.pt. -183 °C).

Why: an insoluble solid in a liquid → filtration; miscible liquids with different boiling points → fractional distillation.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: For each of the following pairs of substances, describe a possible test you would carry out to distinguish between them: (a) sodium chloride and sodium bromide; (b) iron(II) sulfate and copper(II) sulfate; (c) potassium chloride and sodium chloride; (d) zinc chloride and calcium chloride.
exercises.answer: (a) Dissolve each in water, acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate: sodium chloride gives a white precipitate ($AgCl$); sodium bromide gives a cream precipitate ($AgBr$). (b) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide (or aqueous ammonia) to solutions of each: iron(II) sulfate gives a green precipitate; copper(II) sulfate gives a light blue precipitate (which, with excess aqueous ammonia, redissolves to a dark/deep blue solution). The two solutions are also already different colours (pale green vs blue) before any test is even done. (c) Carry out a flame test on each (clean nichrome wire dipped in the solid/solution, then held in a hot Bunsen flame): potassium chloride gives a lilac flame; sodium chloride gives a yellow flame. (d) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide, a little at a time and then in excess, to solutions of each: both first give a white precipitate, but the zinc chloride precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide to give a colourless solution, while the calcium chloride precipitate stays as an insoluble white precipitate. (Aqueous ammonia also works: zinc chloride gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess, whereas calcium chloride gives no precipitate, or only a very slight white one.)
exercises.full_solution:
- **(a)** The anion differs. Dissolve each in water, acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate: sodium chloride gives a **white** precipitate ($\mathrm{AgCl}$), sodium bromide a **cream** precipitate ($\mathrm{AgBr}$).
- **(b)** The cation differs. Add aqueous sodium hydroxide: iron(II) gives a **green** precipitate, copper(II) a **light blue** one, both insoluble in excess. With aqueous ammonia the copper precipitate dissolves in excess to a dark blue solution. The starting solutions are already different colours - pale green and blue.
- **(c)** Both are chlorides, so a silver nitrate test gives the same white precipitate for each. Use a flame test instead on a clean nichrome wire: potassium chloride gives a **lilac** flame, sodium chloride a **yellow** one.
- **(d)** Add aqueous sodium hydroxide a little at a time and then in excess: both give a white precipitate, but the zinc one **dissolves in excess** to a colourless solution while the calcium one stays. With aqueous ammonia, zinc gives a white precipitate soluble in excess and calcium gives no precipitate or only a very slight white one.

Why: pick the test that targets the ion the two substances do not share, and where both give a white precipitate, use what happens on adding excess reagent to tell them apart.
